We predict gravitational waves from binary stellar mergers in nuclear star clusters using an existing formula for binary merger rates. This prediction is based on stellar merger probabilities in various initial mass functions and redshift ranges, which we then apply to understand the potential binary population in the object galaxy of Messier 87 and similar environments. First, we determine the likelihood of specific stellar types found in the M87 globular cluster, and then assess the potential binary population in that cluster and other similar environments. However, our model predicts a binary rate that's two orders of magnitude lower than the gravitational wave signal observed in M87's nucleus, implying that additional dynamics, such as angular momentum conservation, may be at play.

The China Dark Matter Particle Explorer satellite's Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor detected the intense 2022 December 19 GRB, which exceeded any previously recorded brightness. To thoroughly test the robustness of the detector, the full GECAM system was subjected to extreme temperature variations in a vacuum chamber. The structural design of the detector's components was validated through this rigorous testing process. Furthermore, a portable Gamma-Ray Surge simulator has been developed to mimic the actual working conditions of the detector by simulating the December 19 GRB's spectrum and light curve. This simulator allows for precise measurements of the DME's response to extreme events like the GRB, ensuring their reliability in detecting dark matter signals.

This article addresses dynamic systems whose behavior occurs within complex, variable Bergman spaces on the unit disk. It examines how specific operator semigroups affect the L^p and dual BMOA spaces for complex probabilities p greater than one. It demonstrates that for optimal exponents p1 and its dual p2, the operator semigroup preserves BMOA properties. It also investigates a related operator class known as composition-difference operators and determines how this operator impacts BMOA. It demonstrates that composition-difference operators only preserve BMOA properties under specific conditions, notably when the symbol function satisfies certain smoothness criteria similar to those in a specific Sobolev space on the boundary of the unit disk. It extends previous research by relaxing some assumptions and relaxing some conditions, notably when the symbol function meets certain smoothness criteria. It demonstrates that this operator class only preserves BMOa properties under specific conditions, notably when the symbol function satisfies certain smoothness criteria similar to those in a specific Sobolev space on the boundary of the unit disk. It demonstrates that this operator semigroup also impacts a related class of operators known as the Riesz-type operators on the unit disk. It demonstrates that this operator is compact under specific conditions and has the same behavior as identity operator under other conditions.

Historically, the expansive nature of human knowledge facilitated a comfortable human factor in scientific pursuits by enabling rapid accumulation of knowledge. In contrast, across the last half-century, significant breakthroughs in the physical sciences and engineering have been characterized by an exponential growth in data, sensor readings, and model parameters, rather than content. This notable disparity between knowledge quantity and quality highlights the disparity between the massive amount of information and the human factor's role in these fields, suggesting a significant barrier to the future success of AI in the physical sciences and engineering when relying on data-driven approaches. To bridge this gap, the presentation will highlight the disparity between knowledge quantity and quality, examine successful strategies for overcoming this barrier, and explore the potential for human-centric AI within these fields.

In this study, we investigate the security performance of a wireless communication system that utilizes a security-enabled relay to transmit data from an illicit sender to an authorized receiver through an amplitude modulation and demodulation relay. To enhance data transmission efficiency, a multi-carrier approach is employed to simultaneously send multiple data streams from an illicit sender, the authorized receiver, and a eavesdropper, who may intercept data on certain sub-channels, while others remain secure. We analyze various transmission strategies, including those utilizing beamforming and diagonal beamforming matrices, to optimize system security by maximizing the sum security capacity. This optimization takes into account  channel state information known to the illicit sender, the authorized receiver, and the eavesdropper, as well as the constraint that data transmitted on each sub-channel must be non-negative security vulnerable. To achieve this optimal security, we propose an iterative algorithm based on block coordinate descent, which is suitable for the complexity of the underlying non-convex optimization problem. We also evaluate the convergence and computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm. Finally, a numerical example is provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

We examine a quantum system where multiple waveguides are arranged in a ring shape and coated with a layer of material that conducts electricity and emits light, serving as a reservoir. Due to the ring configuration, the system exhibits two distinct phases characterized by the distribution of light modes: either concentrated in the center (symmetric state) or spread along the outer edge (antisymmetric state). In the center phase, interactions between light and the reservoir lead to the creation of mode-specific lattices, while the edge phase confines certain modes to a boundary, forming an effective one-dimensional system that isolates individual light modes. By adjusting the arrangement of the waveguides, we can control the distribution of these modes and even switch between the phases, offering a foundation for developing stable, tunable systems for studying quantum phenomena in light-matter systems.

Developing a predictive control strategy for connected automated vehicles that prioritize safety and utilize data for future traffic management at a marked intersection is a key challenge. To address this challenge, we utilize an Hamilton-Jacobi formulation to create a supervisory controller that prevents rear-end collisions and ensures the safety of pedestrians. This localized guarantee of safety is combined with data-driven optimization of travel time through a Model Predictive Control framework. Furthermore, we explore the balance between optimization and safety by analyzing the impact of PCH region initialization and cost function parameters.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding and reasoning. These complex worlds can also be used to replicate real-world scenarios such as driving and trading. However, current implementations are limited by slow processing speeds, as existing text world engines are hindered by interpretative frameworks that can't keep up with the demands of real-time interactions. Our research introduces a high-performance text world system, which significantly boosts interaction rates by leveraging optimized data structures and pre-trained language models. This new system excels in highly dynamic mazes and intricate navigation challenges, allowing even basic large language models to find solutions.

Deep learning models, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been highly effective in processing and analyzing time-series data.  However, their high computational demands and memory usage have hindered their deployment on energy-efficient hardware.  This research focuses on reducing the size of LSTM models by applying tensor decomposition techniques to both the weight matrices and input data,Packing the computed tensors onto custom FPGA hardware results in a compact and energy-efficient system that outperforms traditional implementations in terms of energy usage per calculation. By integrating tensor decomposition into LSTM algorithms, this work opens up new possibilities for deploying these powerful models on energy-constrained hardware systems.

When training neural networks for NLP, having abundant labeled data is typically a prerequisite for optimal performance. However, many real-world applications involve tasks with only a small amount of available data. Working on a single task with a limited amount of information is known as single-task learning (STL). In contrast, learning multiple tasks at once and applying that knowledge to a task with a limited amount of data is referred to as multi-task learning (MTL). Due to poor STL results under data scarcity, researchers often apply various techniques to enhance STL performance, such as data augmentation, without fully understanding the actual problem. It's worth noting that increasing a neural network's size is also an effective method for improving its performance, even without additional training. Our research involved conducting a comprehensive STL and MTL study using eight widely used NLP datasets with a limited amount of available data. Initially, we assessed the impact of different data augmentation techniques on both STL and MTL performance. Subsequently, we evaluated the influence of neural network architecture and size on both MTL and STL performance. Our results showed that data augmentation techniques have a substantial effect on NLP classification tasks with a limited amount of available data, but this effect is surpassed by increasing the neural network's size.

We demonstrate the validity of a novel hypothesis concerning charged operators in conformal field theory, which implies that their conformal dimensions behave convexly with respect to charge. This new idea has implications for quantum gravity, specifically supporting the controversial "feeble gravity conjecture." We provide a convincing argument for the convexity hypothesis based on the robustness of the Navier-Stokes equation under minor perturbations. Additionally, we explore the connection between this property and the convexity of charged states in quantum mechanics.

To bridge the gap between single-state and multi-state quantum problems, we've developed a novel approach that utilizes a single, comprehensive fictitious time evolution to simultaneously calculate multiple related states. This method, which can be applied to problems involving superconducting quantum interference devices or other similar systems, allows for the calculation of multiple states' evolution over time by employing a 'model space' within the full system's Hilbert space. By focusing on the relevant parts of the system's Hamiltonian, we obtain precise results for the time evolution of multiple states, including scenarios where particles are emitted or absorbed. Our findings demonstrate the method's effectiveness in comparing theoretical predictions with fully exact simulations for various systems over an extended period.

For a specific type of algebraic structure, we've identified a widespread class of indices within that structure, known to exist starting from a certain point. This discovery enables us to establish a connection between the fouling behavior of that structure and the presence of a specific property in certain submodules, with the established relationship being direct. This finding also provides a more applicable basis for proving that certain structures possess the capability to support a specific type of architecture.

The increasing importance of electricity market interdependencies necessitates a more holistic approach to evaluating value-added services. This paper introduces a groundbreaking framework known as the Auxiliary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM), which combines complex market interactions with economic theory to assess the worth of auxiliary services. ASAM employs a mixed integer nonlinear programming method to determine optimal bidding strategies for service providers while considering market interdependencies. A case study using a three-area multi-area test system demonstrates the ASAM's effectiveness and accuracy, especially when compared to traditional optimization approaches. Based on its optimal results, the ASAM provides a foundation for policy makers to design cost-effective allocation strategies for auxiliary services, thereby enhancing grid reliability and efficiency.

We investigate two topics related to F. Gaudry's work from 2009, which required resolving an issue with a prime composition conjecture by confirming specifics about polynomial iteration prime rates. This could potentially be circumvented by proving certain properties about polynomial iteration prime sequences. For comparison, we suggest another prime-related hypothesis based on traditional concepts. Additionally, we examine the original conjecture's validity across various prime categories and explore potential benefits of reducing the proposed condition for prime-prime cases to just prime-squares, which has notable applications in cryptography, particularly in the security of the Galois Counter Mode (GMAC) from the Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) family of algorithms, including AES128-GMAC. We also discuss the feasibility of using specific types of polynomial compositions for generating pseudo-random numbers.

This research applies the matrix element method to investigate Higgs boson pair production at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel where two final-state Higgs bosons decay into top-quarks. We examine a 13 TeV proton-proton collision and consider both standard and beyond-standard models for a comprehensive comparison. Using MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, we simulate a detailed event sample, analyzing it with a Pythia 8 merger to accurately model parton distribution functions and hadronization. We develop an efficient algorithm to handle this complex five-body process, demonstrating its robustness with a 100 fb$^{-1}$ dataset at 13 TeV.

We leverage exact calculations for hadronic $Z$ boson decay and $e^+e^-\to Zh$ processes to test extensions of the Standard Model scalar sector, considering two scenarios: additional dark and heavy $Z$ bosons with identical couplings but different masses. The analysis focuses on experimental data for hadronic $Z$ boson width and cross-section near the Higgs boson mass, and existing constraints on dark and heavy sectors from $Z$ boson pole observables. The study reveals that the dark sector is extensively explored by hadronic $Z$ boson data, while the heavy sector remains largely untested. Furthermore, we examine final states with photon emissions from $Z$ boson decays in the process of $e^+e^-\to \gamma\gamma$ at future linear colliders. The analysis shows that even a precise measurement of the $\sigma(e^+e^-\to Zh)\times BR(h\to bb)$ ratio at a center-of-mass energy of 250 GeV can significantly constrain an untested region of the heavy sector. Additionally, we highlight the potential of full event simulations at 350 GeV and 400 GeV to probe the dark and heavy sectors through $Zh$ events, where the Higgs boson decays into two photons. The simulations indicate that with a sample of 1 ab$^{-1}$, one could find evidence for dark or heavy $Z$

Saturn's polar atmosphere is undergoing a transformation as the sun reaches the planetary equator, causing the north pole to experience continuous darkness. Observations from the Juno spacecraft have provided insights into Saturn's polar dynamics, revealing the development of large-scale heat patterns during Saturn's summer. A persistent swirl of warm gases is now forming near Saturn's north pole, indicative of the summertime polar vortex. This vortex has been observed hovering above Saturn's deep atmosphere and has begun to stretch across multiple latitude bands. Using a sophisticated model, scientists have been able to replicate the movement of Saturn's summertime polar winds and have identified the formation of the vortex as a result of residual warm gases being dragged towards darker regions. These findings suggest that the presence of the vortex is influenced by underlying atmospheric conditions and that it may persist for up to two more Saturn years.

For a specific, non-zero solution $u$ to a time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation, it is demonstrated that under certain conditions, $u$ cannot indefinitely exist outside a bounded, convex area in two or more dimensions. This area is denoted as $\Omega$. When combined with a nonlinear component $\lambda |u|^{p-1}u$, if certain conditions are met for $\lambda$ and $u$, it is shown that $u$ cannot exist for all time. This limitation is further demonstrated to be applicable to a particular type of Schr\"odinger equation that includes a potential $V(x)=d(\text{dist}(x,\Gamma))$, where $d$ is less than one, $\text{dist}(x,\Gamma)$ is the shortest distance from point $x$ to boundary $\Gamma$, and boundary $\Gamma$ is the boundary of the area $\Omega$. This last case is notable for being non-absorbing.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero embedded resolution of singularities can be extended to a wide range of non-characteristic-zero rings, likely including $\mathbb{Z}$, using a new formula-based approach. This method draws from differential algebra and offers a novel perspective on solving this long-standing problem, which has been a significant obstacle in various fields, such as algebraic geometry and number theory.

Investigating V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films, we've discovered an unusual relationship between the metal-insulator transition and surface conditions. Our findings reveal that modifying the surface of the V$_2$O$_3$ film with potassium causes a shift from an insulating to a metallic state, and this transition can be precisely controlled by adjusting the amount of potassium added. Furthermore, our study reveals that the critical angle at which this transition occurs varies in response to potassium doping, and this critical angle is influenced by the balance between electron-electron interactions and electron lattice interactions within the V$_2$O$_3$ film.

We employ both numerical and analytical methods to investigate a quantum double dark-soliton system consisting of two interacting BECs within a single one-dimensional trap. Our findings indicate that as system size increases, separate matter condensations will occur. A simple variational approach is used to accurately predict these results. We also discover that, in the quantum regime, distinct dark holes in the double soliton system may fail to persist due to tunneling between them. This cross-talk can be precisely controlled through the use of an external barrier. A novel method is introduced to create dark-hole like structures in a more practical and feasible manner.

We create a unique linear structure on a linearly homogenous linear bundle associated with a given vector bundle, transforming it into a graded bundle of specific degree. This modification is achieved by expanding the scalar field to include powers. We then establish the properties of these bundles, including their connections and metric systems, and demonstrate how they relate to higher-order geometric frameworks. Notably, we provide a method to solve the absolute parallelism equation for a certain class of connections, revealing an underlying local equivalence to vector bundles.

Let $G$ be a connected reductive algebraic group defined over the rational numbers.  
Let $W$ represent the set of stable orbital integrals on $W(G(\mathbb{R}))$ at a certain prime $p$ where $G$ remains non-singular.  
Let $I_p$ be the space of integral measures on the set of stable orbital integrals at $G(\mathbb{Q}_p)$.  
Our research focuses on the relationship between the sets $I_\mathbb{R}\subset I_\mathbb{Q}_\mathbb{R}$ and $I_p$.  
Given suitable conditions, we can establish a precise formula linking $I_\mathbb{R}$ to $I_\mathbb{Q}_\mathbb{R}$ and $I_p$.

To study the early universe's nuclear synthesis, we propose using x-ray free-electron laser and x-ray spectrometer beamline to perform scattering experiments with monochromatic x-rays. By applying an ultrashort, intense, circularly polarized x-ray pulse to hydrogen gas, we can record time-dependent images that reveal the formation of deuterium and other elements like helium-3 and helium-4. This approach enables visualization of the synthesis process in real-time and may provide insights for improving models of early universe's development.

Quantum error correction is crucial for the success of fault-tolerant quantum computation, yet realistically, both quantum hardware and error correction circuits are subject to noise that can hinder their performance. This paper bridges this gap by creating a unified, non-equilibrium open system model that incorporates encoded quantum information, noisy physical qubits, and classical control. It translates this framework into a quantum spin model and develops a method to study the flow of heat in this system, which is influenced by coupling between different parts of the Heisenberg bath and the addition of thermal engines. Through numerical simulations, it is demonstrated that certain types of quantum error correction codes can successfully protect a quantum bit of information, or even code capacity in the presence of the strong ferromagnetic bias. The study also identifies a key factor that limits the amount of heat that needs to be removed from the system, which has direct implications for the design of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

Recent theoretical predictions have highlighted the remarkable properties of a 2D group-16 element in a tellurene monolayer, which may exhibit large-gap topological characteristics. In this study, we have employed first-principles calculations to explore the structural, electronic, and topological properties of pristine and functionalized tellurene monolayers. Our analysis reveals that various atom-terminations, such as H-, X-, and XX-monolayers (where X represents O, S, Se, and Te), demonstrate stable, gapless electronic properties in the case of pristine tellurene. Conversely, these modified tellurene monolayers display large energy gaps. Specifically, we predict that O- and Se-terminated tellurene possess extraordinary quantum anomalous Hall effects, with quantum anomalous Hall conductances of 2e^2/h and 4e^2/h respectively, making them potential candidates for realizing this phenomenon in 2D materials.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element method for modeling single-phase Darcy flow in a porous medium with embedded fractures. Our method combines a standard mesh representing the porous medium with a specific type of mesh that conforms to the fractures in the medium. The fracture network is modeled using Darcy elements within the fracture mesh and a more complex model based on Bejom elements at the interface between the porous medium and the fracture network. Our approach ensures continuity of certain physical quantities across the two models while allowing for significant reductions in computational resources, even in scenarios involving highly numerous and overlapping fractures. Numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy and versatility of our method for various situations.

We examined the spin current that flows through a spiral magnetic layer when paired with a ferromagnetic contact, finding that it can lead to a switching of the spiral's magnetization. This effect, which occurs more efficiently than in spiral/ferromagnetic setups, allows for a robust switching response. Additionally, the spin current-induced torque on the spiral can be blocked when a ferromagnetic contact aligns with the spiral's magnetization, leading to a significant decrease in the current needed to switch the spiral's state. Finally, we found that a spiral layer can exhibit a unique magnetization precession when exposed to an alternating current through an adjacent ferromagnetic contact, allowing it to act as an oscillatory element. This, when combined with a spiral containing a spiral and a ferromagnetic contact, can lead to a state where the frequency of the precession is locked to the applied current, creating a compact and efficient frequency comb generator.

A Bayes Factor stands as a prominent Bayesian method for outcome decision-making, yet its application is often limited due to concerns regarding extreme values. This issue is frequently attributed to Bayes Factor sensitivity to prior probability choices. Our research reveals that Bayes Factor behavior is influenced by a combination of prior choices and model specifications, rather than just one factor. This discovery paves the way for innovative approaches to navigate Bayes Factor sensitivity, including strategy shifts and adaptive methods. However, many of these approaches remain underutilized. This research identifies five key workflow categories that can guide the development and testing of Bayes Factor strategies. Each category offers a unique perspective on Bayes Factor sensitivity and provides a platform for the creation and evaluation of specific strategies. By focusing on a Bayes Factor sensitivity table, we can design and assess the efficacy of these strategies. This research provides a comprehensive overview of Bayes Factor sensitivity and outlines a path for the development and testing of Bayes Factor strategies.

Discourse markers serve as cues that guide readers in following the logical flow of an argument, facilitating a quicker and more efficient comprehension. However, machine translation systems often fail to accurately capture the specific role of a discourse marker, resulting in translated texts that do not effectively convey the intended meaning. This research proposes a comprehensive suite of tools designed to analyze various aspects of discourse markers, including their function, range, and target in both original and translated languages. When applied to the discourse marker 'donc' in French, this proposed framework demonstrates excellent performance, however, there is still room for improvement, as human judgment remains necessary for evaluating the complex phenomenon of discursion.

We investigated the effects of elevated temperatures on diamond by spectroscopically analyzing the photoluminescence and electron spin resonance of a nitrogen implanted diamond sample containing a known density of defects.  Our experiments were conducted at rates of 100 K to 773 K and varying temperatures.  The photoluminescence spectra and electron spin resonance spectra exhibited a decline as the temperature increased, with distinct changes in the T1 and T2 relaxation times of the T2* and T2 periods.  A rise in T1 was evident above 400 K, with the T2* and T2 periods exhibiting an abrupt increase at 573 K, with the latter increasing by a factor of 10.  In addition, a shift in the electron spin resonance spectrum was evident above 673 K, with the shift being equivalent to a change in g-factor of 0.0002 at 773 K and equivalent to a change in the electron's mass.  Our findings suggest that these findings can be attributed to a change in the lattice structure of diamond and that these results can be applied to a variety of applications, with the most notable being elevated temperature quantum sensing applications.

A novel type of neural network is introduced, based on the self-supervision principle within local areas of the brain. This principle allows a network to learn a precise internal representation, which is then used to predict outcomes and reinforce neural activity. As a result, the network develops meaningful patterns of neural interaction and realistic activity levels. These networks are designed with specific features that mimic real brain cells and utilize a precise model of neural signaling and synaptic plasticity known as STDP. When applied to a network similar to a real brain area, these machines exhibit a high level of detail and are capable of accurately simulating the activity of real brain cells. They also develop a complex pattern of cell activity and firing rates, which are in line with real brain cells. These networks are similar to real brain cells and exhibit a high level of detail and are capable of accurately simulating the activity of real brain cells.

Researchers employed a sigma-model to investigate an $SU(3)$ spin system on a triangular lattice, utilizing a large-$S$ approximation for a Haldane-Shastry type model. By examining the large-$S$ limit through numerical methods, a gap in the spin excitation spectrum was discovered at a specific value of $J$, which is approximately $0.0666\,J_{e}$, where $J_{e}$ is the exchange interaction between spins on adjacent sites of the Haldane-Shastry model. A field-theoretical approach, which is valid for large values of $S$, was also used to locate the critical $J$ value, showing good agreement with the full numerical results. Furthermore, it was suggested that this finding may have implications for the experimentally observed up-down structure in the Li$_{2}$RuO$_{3}$, a material that displays a triangular Ru-O-Ru framework.

A novel implementation of the Hartree-Fock method has been developed, employing B-Spline basis functions to represent wave functions. By utilizing this method, the calculation of both ground and excited state energies and configurations can be performed for systems influenced by central potentials, including atoms, clusters, and electron gas. In this approach, the B-Spline order and knot spacing can be adjusted to optimize the convergence of results, and a significant advantage is that the resulting HF equations can be solved for both ground and excited states with remarkable efficiency. This method has been demonstrated to converge rapidly and yields highly accurate results when applied to both atomic systems and clusters/ electron gas. Notably, it allows for the calculation of both orbitals and exchange matrix elements in a straightforward and efficient manner.

We have developed a universal indicator to identify explosive transitions in coupled oscillator systems where each member of the population exhibits unique characteristics. This indicator is straightforward to calculate and applicable to a broad spectrum of descriptions of singular oscillators. We demonstrate its efficiency by examining the impact of various factors, including time delays, disordered connections, and mesoscale patterns on explosive transitions in coupled oscillator systems.

Matrix factorization methods have been extensively applied to resolve a variety of challenging, convex or nonconvex optimization problems. This study investigates the difficult landscape of general nonconvex matrix optimization problems, specifically those involving minimization over positive definite matrices, by applying a Riemannian framework. By examining the geodesic curvature and Hessians at critical points, we identify a set of "geodesically convex" regions, where the number of negative directions in the Hessian is limited, and prove that any local minimum lies within one of these regions. This analysis has significant implications for optimizing low-rank matrices, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our findings by applying them to check the landscape of specific problems, such as nuclear norm maximization and positive definite matrix completion. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the global landscape of nonconvex matrix optimization problems.

Recently, Kahn and Szeptycki robustly proved a conjecture by Erdos about edge-coloring in large, dense, bipartite graphs that approach the bound set by a counterexample to the Chandler conjecture. This work presents the first known robust version of its class. We provide a response to the Erdos-Sos conjecture by presenting a bipartite graph with a specific structure that cannot be edge-colored with a certain number of colors according to its expected properties. This graph also invalidates a conjecture by Alon, Tarsi, and others regarding the chromatic index of dense graphs.

Let $q$ be an integer greater than one, and let $\chi$ be a Dirichlet character modulo $q$. Our research will focus on the novel identities associated with the odd integer-based Dirichlet $L$-functions.

The Standard Model of particle physics is a well-established scientific achievement, yet its underlying principles are still debated. To uncover new particles, the LHC has been a key tool, but it is limited to finding particles with masses up to several TeV. To overcome this barrier, we propose combining particle physics and cosmology to search for particles up to 10^9 GeV. We suggest that defects formed after the Big Bang, like scalar field ones, could produce extremely long, thin, and temperature-controlled wires in the universe. These wires would create high temperatures that could cause the wires to break, but not directly. Instead, their decay products would result in very high-energy particles. The number of these particles could be controlled by the temperature of the universe, and their distribution would be influenced by the particles' properties. A key limitation is that these particles would be affected by the universe's expansion, and their detection would depend on their interaction with other matter. We suggest that they could be detected indirectly through their effect on high-energy gamma rays, or directly through their effect on charged particles in the universe. As an example, we show that these particles could be detected if they interact with other matter in a specific way, or if they are charged and their magnetic field is strong.

A significant number of proteins found in nature adopt an asymmetric structure, with a notable fraction exhibiting a directional preference. These enzymes often contain multiple binding sites for fuel, which can be arranged in various ways to optimize their swimming speed in a gel that resists flow. It has been established that viscoelasticity has a significant effect on the swimming speed of such traps, with the underlying mechanism still a topic of ongoing research. In order to better understand this phenomenon, we performed numerical simulations using a molecular dynamics model that accounted for the mesh physics of polymer networks. Our results indicated that the general impact of viscoelasticity on the swimming speed of a helical structure is quite a bit more complex than previously thought and is heavily influenced by the design of the structure. In the case of a directional preference, viscoelasticity has a significant effect on the swimming speed, with the structure adapting its shape to the environment. Our findings also revealed that there is a critical point in which the swimming speed is quite a bit slower than in a Newtonian fluid, with the exact point being determined by the ratio of shear and extensional resistance. In order to avoid this phenomenon, we found that increasing the extensional resistance to a certain level has a significant effect on the swimming speed, with the exact level being quite a bit more complex and still being determined.

We investigated whether evolutionary processes can lead a group of learning players in a Cournot market to a Nash equilibrium. We developed a genetic algorithm to model this and found that it can indeed converge to the exact or near-exact molar flow rate that would maximize the market's profit. This RGA method demonstrated stability and resilience, with minimal variation and recovery capacity when disrupted. We found that as the number of traders increases, an RGA solution approaches the theoretical Nash equilibrium, according to Bertrand Deacon's theorem.

The growing demand for OAE resources necessitates a robust and efficient
information extraction framework that can adapt to various languages and
domains. To achieve this, we propose a novel and efficient extraction method
that leverages state-of-the-art natural language processing techniques to
identify and integrate world knowledge from unstructured text into ontologies.
Our approach utilizes a deep learning model based on Long Short-Term Memory
networks, which processes text and generates precise entity boundaries and
classification through a detailed analysis of character-level inputs. This model
is further optimized by incorporating the Attention mechanism to enhance
performance and produce more accurate results. Experimental results on English
text demonstrate the model's ability to produce high-quality F1 scores of up to
94.55%, and its adaptability to other languages and domains makes it a valuable
framework for ontology expansion.

On a fully interconnected graph, we doped an Ising model with a subset of 'garbage' variables to create nonequilibrium systems driven by a flow of heat from the 'doped' sites to the Ising spins, which act as a heat sink. We found that, in contrast to fully nonequilibrium models, these hybrid systems display phases that resemble those found in equilibrium. When the 'doping' level drops below a certain threshold, the system's behavior is highly dependent on the type of garbage used.

Understanding how viruses spread through the air is crucial for effective disease prevention and control, especially given the global impact of recent respiratory illnesses. This study employs theoretical models and computer simulations to examine the complexity of air-borne virus transmission influenced by various weather conditions. Our analysis highlights that weather changes significantly alter the settling and degradation rates of virus-laden air droplets, leading to varying outcomes in virus spread under different environmental conditions. Specifically, our results indicate that lower temperatures and reduced humidity can prolong the viability of certain viruses, while moderate levels of sunlight have a lesser effect on their rate of spread. This research underscores the importance of taking into account environmental factors in public health strategies and emphasizes the need for further study to better comprehend the dynamics of air-borne virus transmission.

The rate of data generation in physics experiments and theoretical calculations is being significantly increased by the continuous advancements in technology. To keep pace with this rapid growth, machine learning methods such as neural networks are being increasingly applied in theoretical and experimental physics. However, one challenge that remains is their inability to accurately assess prediction uncertainty, which could have serious implications for their reliability. Despite the general knowledge of uncertainty measurement in traditional machine learning, there's a lack of transferable understanding to the specialized fields of physics and science. To bridge this gap, we've developed a comprehensive framework that includes various uncertainty quantification techniques tailored for neural machine learning models based on next-generation machine infrastructure, allowing for the systematic evaluation of their performance through extensive numerical numerical experiments. Our experiments involve large-scale numerical simulations and theoretical and data-driven models, which take into account covariance effects and are informed by the characteristics of machine infrastructure, such as ill-conditioned matrices. As a result, we've identified the most effective methods for predicting regression targets and class memberships with the lowest loss functions and highest accuracy, respectively.

Given a weighted directed graph $\mathcal{D}$ and a positive integer $k$, we define the $k$-th power of the edges of $\mathcal{D}$, denoted as $\mathcal{D}^k$, and investigate the boundedness of the sequence of its edge ideal powers. We also establish a bound for the regularity of the sequential powers of $\mathcal{D}^k$'s edge ideal.

Quantum matrix models based on two $N\times N$ matrices exhibited a unique feature at specific values of $N$, where the Bethe ansatz could explain all their properties. This study aimed to extend the proposed duality between these matrix models and deformed $S^5$ super-Yang-Mills theory to include finite values of $N$. By applying a method that accommodates the discrete nature of the theory at finite $N$, a set of equations was derived to describe the theory's non-perturbative aspects. These equations include a newly formulated "Bethe equation" and an additional constraint, which was interpreted as a result of magnetic flux conservation. A simpler set of equations was also obtained for polynomial-like states, with one instance corresponding to a modified form of the TQ relation.

Deep learning-based computer vision systems, particularly those utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have significantly advanced and are now being adopted for both research and commercial purposes. However, these sophisticated algorithms are susceptible to hardware malfunctions that can lead to catastrophic failures. Although various techniques exist to mitigate such errors in traditional computing, many are resource-intensive and lack the adaptability required for CNNs. This paper presents the initial stage of developing a structured framework to justify the safe operation of hardware-fault resilient CNNs through activation range supervision, while addressing current limitations and highlighting necessary enhancements.

The banking system's complexity has led to a novel approach, leveraging blockchain for end-user transactions, which has now been explored in a non-financial setting. A specific scenario is presented where the Romanian Ministry of Economy requires an effective method to manage financial debts among companies in various sectors of the economy. Three potential solutions are proposed, which are evaluated based on functionality, performance, security, and cost, resulting in selection of a specific architecture based on a process diagram and an AUMLA protocol. This solution integrates a data format, a blockchain protocol, and a specific application of a consensus mechanism, which has been assessed using a case study and demonstrates efficiency, liveness, and robustness, indicating its potential for implementing a partial system prototype.

Researchers have previously identified various Jordanian twist deformations of the universal R-matrix for $SL_q(2)$, but they have not exhaustively covered all possible adjustments. This study presents a comprehensive method to derive an extensive set of Jordanian twist R-matrices from an origin R-matrix, specifically for $SL_q(2)$. This method not only provides explicit deformation formulas but also confirms its validity through direct verification.

We've developed a novel, language-agnostic word representation technique that efficiently transfers linguistic knowledge from a multitude of languages.  Our approach, which builds a common semantic space across a variety of languages with minimal computation, effectively groups words from different languages based on their shared meanings rather than their surface forms.  By leveraging a single, universally applicable objective function, our method achieves a high level of accuracy in embedding quality, surpassing existing methods on a range of benchmark evaluations.  Moreover, our approach excels in tasks that require the combination of semantic information with other data sources, such as the matching of pairs of sentences.  Notably, our model can be fine-tuned for specific applications by adjusting a single, task-specific parameter.  We've discovered that our clustering technique yields a more robust and consistent set of word embeddings, even when there are discrepancies in the training data.  By aggregating the latent spaces of individual language models, we've created a common semantic area that excels in a variety of linguistic tasks, including word analogies, integration of words and sentences, and the translation of sentences.  Our results indicate substantial improvements in accuracy across all evaluated tasks, with notable gains in the difficulty of sentence integration.  We attribute these improvements to our technique's ability to learn a more coherent and consistent set of word representations, thereby facilitating the efficient combination of semantic information with other data sources.

This paper outlines the production of various particles, including pions, kaons, protons, and phi mesons, in Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.44 TeV. The particle yields are based on simulations and experimental data, which show that pions are primarily produced through quark interactions, while kaons are also significantly produced through quark interactions. Protons are mainly produced through quark interactions, with a minor contribution from parton interactions. Phi mesons are produced through quark interactions and are in thermal equilibrium with the surrounding particles.

A significant barrier to building conversational agents that automate complex tasks is the lack of high-quality, large-scale datasets for training dialogue state tracking models. Most existing datasets are gathered from human-human conversations, which are prone to inaccuracies, and are often manually annotated, resulting in limited size and inability to capture multi-turn conversations. Furthermore, these datasets include implicit information within the conversations that is frequently overlooked. In this study, we present the ASSIST dataset, an extensive DST training dataset consisting of over 100,000 conversations across eight distinct domains. It includes both explicit and implicit information, as well as labels that account for the noise present within the conversations. In our experiments, models trained on the ASSIST dataset outperform those using widely used benchmark datasets, demonstrating the potential of the proposed dataset.

In late October 2019, protests in Chile escalated following a fatal incident during demonstrations, quickly spreading to other major cities and disrupting the country's infrastructure. To comprehend and address such events, a new mathematical model was devised to analyze historical data and mitigate adverse effects. This new approach considers migrants entering major cities from smaller ones, based on the ratio of people leaving major cities to those leaving smaller cities. The resulting predictions matched observed patterns during the protests, with observed data being used to parameterize the model.

We investigated the reliability of using spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting to determine galaxy star formation rates (SFRs) by comparing its results to those obtained from various single-method techniques. To do this, we employed a data-driven approach to establish both a high and low threshold for expected SFR values, which served as benchmarks for evaluating the accuracy of different methods. We then compared SED-fitting-derived SFRs to those derived from measurements of specific spectral lines, line line-ratios, line line-stokes parameters, line line-equivalent widths, and lines that are robust against line contamination. We found that different methods performed well at lines beyond the line-break, but struggled at shorter wavelengths. The line-based approaches generally matched the low and high thresholds at lines beyond the line-break, but frequently failed to do so at shorter wavelengths. The line-based methods also tended to overestimate SFRs at lines between the line-break and hydrogen lines. The line-based star formation indicators generally agreed with each other at galaxies beyond the line-break, but often diverged significantly at shorter wavelengths. The line-based SFRs were also observed to be systematically lower than the line-based SFRs at hydrogen lines. The line-based SFRs were also observed to be systematically lower than the line-based SFRs at galaxies beyond the line-break, but frequently failed to do so at shorter wavelengths. The line-based SFRs also tended to overestimate SFRs at lines between the line-break and hydrogen

We are studying a notable boundary between the SOS cone in R^n and its interior, specifically its (n-1)-dimensional surface. Our main achievement is providing a clear, one-dimensional basis for this surface when n is up to nine. Additionally, we're able to fill in some previously known gaps in research, especially for four-dimensional space. Our approach involves using strictly positive polynomials that remain positive even when evaluated at a small neighborhood around any point on this surface. It's interesting to note that our method doesn't depend on any complex properties of the boundary itself.

This paper addresses a critical challenge in verifying concurrent systems by extending regular expression constraints, which are a fundamental tool for analyzing the behavior of programs. Although previous methods using regular expressions have successfully identified bugs in various software systems, their applicability is limited due to the absence of techniques for concurrent language constructs like parallel execution and conditional logic. Building on a proposed framework for analyzing concurrent programs, this work extends regular expression constraints to incorporate these missing constructs and introduces an innovative approach to symbolically determining solutions for these constraints. A Prolog library has been created to implement this solving technique, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness through the detection of bugs in both benchmark systems and actual software, including a case where a bug was found in a deployed service.

To accelerate the ongoing industrial adoption of neural network-based localization systems, this research develops an innovative approach called External Memory Attention Virtual-inertial localization. By integrating an external memory attention mechanism, our method excels in processing high-frame rate input video streams at a rate of 90 frames per second, even when optimal inertial measurements are unavailable. Our approach outperforms existing industry standards in speed and processing efficiency, exhibiting superior accuracy in stream evaluations and robust performance in stream-rover testing scenarios.

Quantum Hall effects in ordinary Weyl materials stem from the linear dispersion seen in Weyl materials. In contrast, order-parameter-dependent Weyl materials will see their quantum Hall states depend on different orders of a symmetry-broken parameter, much like in BCS superconductors.

This study examines a problem of reconstructing missing information in a given 3D domain for Maxwell's equations, where the boundary values and part of the internal electric field are known. A time-periodic scenario is analyzed, and the corresponding quasi-reversibility method is both derived and justified mathematically. Key aspects of the regular and degenerate cases for the target function are discussed, and the direct, least-squares, and Tikhonov penalty TQR methods are described. Initial and final error bounds for these TQR variants are established. A novel TQR approach using discontinuous finite elements is proposed and its convergence rate is proved. The results are supported by two-dimensional numerical examples.

This paper builds on the work of H. Huang and H.-S. Zhang by establishing the integral conjugation and internal object morphism properties for the module category of the parafermion vertex operator algebra $K(osp(1|2n),k)$. As a consequence, we derive the modular transformation rules for its fusion space matrix and confirm the configuration of its fusion category.

In today's technology-driven world, large-scale machine learning models are being used extensively to generate high-quality machine learning models for various applications. Despite their success, these pre-trained models come with a significant cost, which is why many organizations choose to train models from scratch on smaller datasets. This paper proposes a novel approach called FCKA, which allows multiple stakeholders to seamlessly train and combine a machine learning model from their respective data sources without revealing their underlying datasets to one another or paying a costly machine learning model. To achieve this, the KGA module uses a machine learning model to identify and combine data that is similar across stakeholders, which in turn improves the quality of the trained machine learning model. To protect the security of the process, the KSA module verifies that only authorized stakeholders are involved in the process.

Eight years have passed since the discovery of entorhinal cortex (EC) grid cells in rats, which were found to be grid neurons located in the medial EC (MEC). Following this breakthrough, researchers worldwide have been actively investigating grid neurons, utilizing both behavioral experiments and computational models to explore their underlying mechanisms. A comprehensive survey of grid neuron research has yet to be compiled. Our review covers advancements made over the past eight years in grid neuron research, including development of technologies for noninvasive imaging of grid neurons and their axon terminals, as well as improvements in understanding how axon terminals respond to stimulation and image reconstruction. Moreover, we discuss recent progress in modeling the formation and maintenance of grid patterns.

Research on solar and stellar rotation shows that rotation rates decrease from the equator to the poles, a phenomenon known as differential rotation. This paper delves into how this variation in rotation affects solar and star behavior, focusing on rotation rates above and below the critical value for magnetic field generation. We conducted experiments using a 3D simulation to examine the impact of rotating turbulence on magnetic field creation in objects with different rotation profiles. Our analysis revealed a significant decrease in magnetic field generation as the simulation approached the critical point of rotation. We then developed a statistical model to examine the relationship between magnetic field generation and rotation. This model indicated that objects with lower rotation rates would generate more magnetic fields, a phenomenon opposite to what is observed on the Sun. We then explored how this model could be applied to understand magnetic cycles in stars and discovered that it could help explain the magnetic behavior of some stars, but not all.

We examine how the elliptic curves of the form E/Q behave in the contexts of two specific Galois-invariant subcurves E1/Q1 E2/Q2 without rational points, which lead to fields K of the type A4 or S4, with a quartic basis, over which the rank increases by at least 1. As a result, under certain hypotheses regarding the parity of points, we demonstrate that the average rank increment across all such K is at least 5/6 for A4 and at least 4/3 for S4. Furthermore, we provide an estimate for the average rank increment across all such K that lies in extensions of the rationals with a Galois group of Sd, with d greater than or equal to 4.

Unitary quantum systems can only increase their entropy through a maximum flux determined by their operators' mutual information with the rest of the system, a principle known as the quantum null energy condition. Investigating a quantum null slice in AdS/CFT, we find a quantum surge that directly corresponds to the surge's geometric properties. We then apply this understanding to quantify the growth rate of entanglement in a boundary CFT by examining the quantum surge of a Rindler horizon, finding that a plucking primary heavy operator operation leads to an entanglement growth rate proportional to a central charge combination.

We investigate the relationship between asymmetric quantum correlations and quantum speed limits using nonlocal distinguishing games. Our analysis reveals that a longer duration for distinguishing operations in this context corresponds to greater system asymmetry. Specifically, we employ an asymmetry monotone, the Jarzynsky skew information, to quantify system asymmetry. Utilizing this measure, we establish a direct inequality between average speed limits and asymmetry during unitary evolution within the Bloch ball. Our findings can serve as a benchmark for quantum sensors and memory devices with asymmetry-modulating properties. Our work extends previous research on distinguishing operations to operations that are biased.

The primary objective of this research is to provide a practical method for calculating the one-norm of the interpolation projector associated with bivariate $L$-orthogonal polynomials. We have developed an iterative approach to estimate the Interpolation Lag Multiplier (ILM) matrix's one-norm, thereby enabling the determination of the interpolation projector's one-norm for any family of $L$-orthogonal polynomials. This method is particularly useful in scenarios where some components of the ILM matrix's one-norm are difficult to compute analytically. An examination of the asymptotic behavior of the interpolation norms is also explored. Additionally, an examination of the asymptotic behavior of the interpolation norms is conducted, and the exact interpolation norms for the $(d+1)^2$ points derived from the generalized Gaussian quadrature is proved to be one. Furthermore, an estimation of the interpolation projector's one-norm for the modified Bessel functions of the first kind of integer order is performed.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as leading platforms for quantum computing, yet they are vulnerable to external electromagnetic interference due to their vulnerable nature. Although it is possible to harness this susceptibility to create highly sensitive sensors, it is crucial to understand and minimize the sources of noise within these sensors and any nearby devices. In this study, we used terahertz nanoscopy to examine the spatial distribution of currents in superconducting resonators that are part of a sensor, as well as in nearby superconducting wires. By comparing experimental results with simulations, we obtained a precise description of the electromagnetic field, allowing us to identify potential areas of concern. Notably, we found that residual resistances can cause significant field distortions, hindering a clear understanding of the coupling between the sensor and any quantum bits. Furthermore, we found that a/2 spacing between wires is optimal for minimizing mutual inductance and preventing mode mixing. This investigation provides a method for experimentally optimizing the designs of sensors and other superconducting devices to ensure their reliable performance.

We introduce a new theory, $\mathrm{KKR}$, which computes algebraic $K$-groups for a specific type of algebraic variety through a combination of motivic spectra and invertible sheaves on those varieties. Our approach builds upon a previous discovery that connects algebraic $K$-theory to effective motivic spectra, providing $\mathrm{KKR}$ as a derived version of "curved line bundles" within the motivic framework. The theory $\mathrm{KKR}$ exhibits key properties, including invariance under motivic equivalence, Glueing, and the satisfaction of curved Chern character and change of ring formulas, ultimately facilitating the computation of $K$-theory for some algebraic varieties.

This work examines the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, considering various factors that influenced its development. These include volcanic activity, surface material, atmospheric changes, and space environment, as well as their interplay. Current research indicates that Venus's atmosphere likely went through significant transformations, with different stable states possible. However, existing models could not accurately predict the planet's current atmosphere. We propose that complex processes, including abrupt shifts and environmental and geological feedback mechanisms, contributed to its evolution.

A novel technique combines nanoscopy and nuclear reactions to create an all-optical method for controlling and emitting glycol ions from minuscule droplets as small as 10 micrometers in diameter. Using linear glycol targets, this method can also measure the speed distribution of the emitted ions, which are highly sensitive to the droplet's surface properties. By applying linear carbon beams, the nanoscopy reveals a linear speed distribution for the emitted glycol ions, which can be influenced by adding hygroscopic salts to the glycol. The emitted glycol ions offer a potential means to design better glycol-based sensors and explore new ways to understand and manipulate supercooled substances.

Researchers have recently developed an innovative concept called "Superficial Quantum Circuits" (SQC) to decompose two key representations, like Projected Entangled Pair Operators (PEPS) and Matrix Product States (MPS), widely used to model two and one dimensional lattice systems respectively. We provide a fresh, user-friendly approach to reconstructing the SQC from a given MPS, utilizing distinct state and circuit building blocks to represent the state's properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that modifications to the SQC's underlying QC can be employed to achieve a more optimal decomposition of the MPS, by leveraging the flexibility in swappable operations characteristic of SQCs.

The creation of algorithms that automatically analyze medical images is a crucial area of development for computer-aided diagnosis systems. These algorithms are particularly important in pathology, where evaluating tissue samples involves assessing numerous features across multiple spatial scales. To tackle this multi-level problem, researchers have recently turned to hierarchical convolutional neural networks. This approach enables them to capture relationships between different parts of a pathology sample and how those parts contribute to understanding the whole. Building on this work, we propose a new hierarchical network framework that utilizes a unique hierarchical graph structure to represent the connections within a tissue sample. We also present a corresponding training framework called HIERO, which combines a hierarchical attention mechanism and a multi-level loss function. Experiments on three cancer datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 5.4% and a average hierarchy attention score increase of 10.1%. To aid future research, a web platform is made available to facilitate the testing of algorithms.

This paper provides an overview of our implementation of a non-linear Hawkes process model, which is difficult to analyse due to its lack of analytical solutions for key statistics. We present a Bayesian approach using probabilistic programming, specifically Pyro, to develop a flexible model that can be flexibly evaluated. Our method uses approximate Bayesian computation to obtain approximate posterior distributions and estimated parameters. We demonstrate the model's efficacy in estimating parameters for real-world data, and show that a non-linear model offers a significant improvement over a linear baseline.

Engaging systems comprising numerous identical objects can be efficiently calculated by combining the multipole expansion with second-order numerical methods. This technique, known as the Fast Multipole Method, has an irrotational character however and therefore cannot accurately represent scenarios that involve the preservation of angular momentum and rotationally singular densities. We enhance the traditional second-order FM^2 method to incorporate an additional term that ensures the conservation of angular momentum. This enhanced version, called the First-order Fast Multipole Method with angular momentum preservation (FFM), enables a more precise approximation of rotationally singular densities. We demonstrate that FM^2 and FFM converge at rates of O(h^2) and O(h), respectively. FF^M also exhibits superiority over FM^2 in certain scenarios that pertain to angular momentum preservation however FM^2 remains a preferable alternative for general applications. FFM also demonstrates a capability to converge at a linear rate to solutions that FM^2 cannot capture due to its inherent lack of angular momentum conservation.

Although deep learning-based segmentation models have been successfully applied in multiple medical imaging modalities, they still face significant challenges due to the issues of image variability and data scarcity. One possible solution to overcome these issues is Domain Adaptive Segmentation (DAS), which allows for training models on a limited number of labeled images from a source domain and adapting them to an unlimited number of unlabeled target domain images. However, most previous research on DAS has primarily focused on a single modality and failed to explore multi-modal settings. In addition, existing single-modal DAS methods often struggle with satisfactory performance when adapting images from a limited number of target samples. In this research, we address these limitations by proposing a novel domain adaptive learning framework that addresses both single and multi-modal settings and allows for adaptation from limited target samples. Our proposed framework combines contrastive semi-supervised learning and a contrastive loss function to capture the contextual relationships between a limited number of labeled target images and a large number of self-supervised consistency-consistent target images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework by presenting results on two datasets with different anatomical structures, showing significant improvements in metrics such as mean surface distance and Dice similarity coefficient compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.

The foundation of modern gauge theory, established by Faddeev and Popov in 1966 through the path integral method, relies on a specific mathematical representation known as the 2nd order formalism. This framework is characterized by describing the gauge group using its algebra and the associated generators. In contrast, supergravity involves a more intricate structure that encompasses both algebraic and geometric aspects of the gauge group. Due to these additional requirements, the Faddeev-Popov approach cannot be directly applied to supergravity. Furthermore, attempting to incorporate ghost fields within the supergravity path integral leads to inconsistencies, as it would result in a violation of the BRS symmetry transformation.

To improve the efficiency of polarization alteration in high-power laser pulses, a novel approach is proposed by combining specific plasma structures with an external magnetic field. Through simulation using 1D and 2Plas codes, it is demonstrated that this method can effectively rotate the polarization state of high-power laser pulses while also providing significant energy gain. The approach is applicable to a wide range of input powers and frequencies, with the ability to control both rotation angle and energy gain through plasma structure and density optimization. Notably, the proposed method is capable of handling extremely high powers up to 100 petawatts across a wide bandwidth, with subsequent applications in high-efficiency radiation generation and polarization control in advanced plasma-based technologies.

To constrain the dipole form factors of the $\tau$ lepton, a new and robust method is proposed, enabling a rigorous data analysis. By examining $e^+e^-\to \tau^+\tau^-$ events collected at center-of-mass energies below the production threshold, a technique is developed to accurately identify and count $\tau$ decays, even when both particles decay. Utilating this approach, limits on the magnitude of the dimensionful electric dipole form factor are obtained. Assuming the vector and axial-vector couplings align with the standard model predictions, the current data from Belle allow the most stringent $\tau$ electric dipole form factor bounds to be derived, reaching an upper bound of $|f_E(s_\tau)]/f_A(s_\tau)] < 4.0 \times 10^{-4}$ at a 90% confidence level.

This paper proposes a decoding method for rank metric code errors that have a symmetry property. A rank metric error matrix with this property can be represented by two permutation vectors, and we develop decoding algorithms capable of finding these vectors to recover the original message. Firstly, a probabilistic algorithm is proposed to locate the two permutation vectors, and subsequently, a new decoding method is developed based on this proposal. Moreover, a specific family of rank metric codes, which have systematic parity check matrix generator based on Cauchy matrix properties, is introduced. These codes demonstrate that the symmetric decoding method offers performance comparable to that of generic decoding, which outperforms only maximum likelihood ranking, providing a compelling justification for the proposed symmetric rank metric application model.

Building on the work of de Boer, Denef, and Prats, our study delves into the conformal field theory (CFT) side of the AdS$_3$/CFT$_3$ duality, specifically examining operator product expansions (OPEs) and how they relate to protected sets of operators, or operators that don't change under the Weyl anomaly. We provide a detailed analysis of a specific $sl(2|1)$ super-Wess-Zumino-Witten model, an $sl(2)$ supersymmetric extension of the WZW model, and its long-established duality with massive type IIA supergravity on the AdS$_3 \times S^3 \times T^4$ background. We then construct the spin-Wilson line, associated with the OPE of primary superfields in the super-CFT, and its correspondence with a supergravity description of two supergravitinos interacting through a non-abelian gauge field, or the super-Kaluza-Klein vector. We then derive a key identity that holds for all masses, which equates the CFT four-point function to its supergravity counterpart, thereby confirming an earlier conjecture made by de Boer, Denef, and Prats.

A significant barrier in analyzing Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations is the distortion caused by large-scale structure lensing. To effectively study inflation and other cosmological phenomena, researchers must "delense" the CMB anisotropies. This delensing process is equivalent to reconstructing the lensing effect and subtracting it out. We developed a method for delensing that utilizes a neural network to model the relationship between large-scale structure and CMB anisotropies. Our approach excels at extracting information about the graviton spectrum from "B-mode" mode spectra that have been distorted by lensing. When 2 billion Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) galaxies are combined with CMB data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and Planck, our neural network-based delensing method recovers tensor modes with 2.5 times more precision than conventional quadratic delensing techniques. This method retains its performance regardless of the foreground contamination in CMB data or the correlation between observed galaxies and early universe fluctuations. When applied to CMB-only data, our technique achieves delensing equivalent to combining CMB with a virtual survey of 20 trillion sources, vastly exceeding current and near-future capabilities for large-scale structure surveys.

In 1991, Gelfand and MacPherson established a recursive method for determining the Pontrjagin classes of any manifold, based on the way submanifolds are combined. Here, I will expand upon this result by providing a direct formula instead of relying on the combinatorial approach.

We obtained optical spectra and photometry for SN 2020jfo, a Type II-plateau supernova, located in NGC 4736. It occurred in an early-type star within a low-luminosity dwarf galaxy, and its peak brightness was moderate, around -17. SN 2020jfo displayed typical characteristics of SN II, including a prominent H-alpha emission line in its early spectrum, but its light curve and colors diverged from normal SN II-P. It exhibited a rapid decline in the peak of its light curve and an unusual increase in the U band after day 20. SN 2020jfo's spectrum at 100 days post-explosion resembled that of SN 2005gl, which is thought to be a result of a massive star collision.

To address the lack of large-class X-ray detectors capable of wide-field spectral analysis, an effective wide-field X-ray spectral monitoring technique needs to be developed. One promising approach involves combining X-ray optical systems with standard X-ray detectors, specifically by modifying how they focus X-rays. By reorienting multiple small grazing-incidence mirrors into parallel rows and adding a thick detector behind them, even small detectors like silicon CCDs can achieve wide-field spectral monitoring capabilities. This concept of modified optics can be applied in various configurations, including micro-lobster and flat-blobster setups, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. Notable successful implementations of grazing-incidence mirror optical systems combined with standard X-ray detectors include the IXHE on Chandra and the lobster-eye camera on Swift, but there is room for further optimization of mirror systems to maximize detector usage and reduce data processing requirements. A thorough examination of several mirror-detector combinations at multiple X-ray energies has been conducted through detailed simulations, assessing factors such as effective area, spectral range, data processing demands, and system robustness. These simulations have been applied to specific mirror-detector setups, including micro-lobster and flat-blobster configurations, and considered several possible uses for these systems in wide-field X-ray monitoring applications, with a focus on large-scale systems that could be achieved in the coming decade.

We establish that a level set level function for a class of second-order uniformly elliptic linear or nonlinear divergence form operators with divergence coefficient(s) satisfies an optimal regularity condition on its boundary, under given assumptions. This relationship is level set based, where the operator leads to the divergence equation and the relatively new level set approach offers an alternative to traditional methods. Notably, the divergence operator in our proof can be time-dependent, which has an application to regularity and optimal growth conditions of the boundary in time for the associated divergence equation.
