This project proposes a novel semi-supervised convolutive non-negative matrix factorization (CNMF) approach using a time-domain analysis to automatically score musical pieces from a recording. Using two convoluted filters to simulate the impulse response of a real keyboard, our method stands out by training only on a few recorded notes from the instrument, thus overcoming limitations of CNN-based methods that require training on multiple instruments. This approach was successfully applied to score two pieces from the piano, including the Petroff sonata and the Beethoven's piece 32 in C minor.

A new mathematical framework has been developed to study the evolution of rotating stars under general relativity, addressing issues with previous methods that used coordinate angles to describe star rotation. The new approach utilizes a coordinate system based on fluid flow, making it applicable to both rotating and non-rotating stars. Furthermore, this formulation preserves the underlying mathematical structure known as symmetry when converting equations into an integrodifferential form. The integration of these factors results in a more efficient and accurate numerical solution, evident from the high-precision data presented in the accompanying graph.

A key challenge in extracting information from visually complex documents like invoices and forms is obtaining a large amount of accurately labeled training data. Our novel approach, called Unsupervised Learning with Visually Rich Documents (ULVR), overcomes this limitation by allowing an extraction model to learn from a small amount of unlabelled data. Unsupervision significantly simplifies the data collection process and leads to excellent performance gains, particularly when training data is limited. Contrary to existing methods that attempt to train models without labels using self-correction techniques, our framework is based on a clean learning setup and employs an unsupervised preprocessing step to improve representation before the extraction model is trained with minimal amounts of labeled data through active learning. Our results show that our unsupervised step significantly boosts the final accuracy, particularly in scenarios with limited data availability.

The detection of gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences has the potential to provide significant insights into the field of general relativity and astrophysics. This paper presents a novel application of deep learning techniques to automatically identify neutron star-black hole mergers, using the full waveform data. The developed deep learning network, based on complex-valued convolutional neural architecture, achieves high accuracy in detecting gravitational waves from neutron star-black hole mergers under various conditions. This approach overcomes previous limitations imposed by simulation data and showcases the efficiency of deep learning techniques in this field. The paper also explores the classification of the remnant objects resulting from compact binary coalescences, using the same high-accuracy deep learning network. The results indicate that this approach outperforms traditional methods in accuracy, especially in cases where the mass ratio between the objects is close to one. The paper also discusses the use of tensor lyra spectra to visualize the decision boundaries of the deep learning model, providing a deeper understanding of its classification capabilities. Overall, this research contributes to the advancement of gravitational wave data analysis techniques and highlights the potential of deep learning techniques in this field.

In the age of information, healthcare professionals are faced with an ever-growing deluge of data. To navigate this challenge, a high-quality healthcare information system is essential for enhancing decision-making processes and addressing complex problems. With advancements in natural language processing and information extraction technology, it's now feasible to automatically generate these high-quality information systems from vast amounts of unstructured text data. This process, known as large-scale structured information extraction, has significant potential in various healthcare domains, particularly in identifying social determinants of health (SDOH) to support value-based care. This paper introduces a novel multi-task information extraction framework that leverages state-of-the-art language models and attention-based components to structurally extract SDOH from electronic health records (EHRs). Building upon this, we also develop a two-stage quality information system that first focuses on accurately linking relevant SDOH mentions to individual patients, and then employs a multi-layer long short-term memory (LSTM) model to extract relevant SDOH information. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this system, it is applied to a real-world dataset of over 1.2 million de-identified visits from a major US healthcare system. Experimental results reveal that the proposed quality information system outperforms existing methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1 score, achieving a remarkable improvement of 10.41% in terms of overall quality F1 score.

This research builds upon a previous study by H. K. Zhang, which developed a method to determine the optimal shape and movement of a two-dimensional scallop within an incompressible, viscous fluid under the Reynolds number of 1. A scallop is used as a basic model to study how small swimmers move in the viscious fluid. Due to the absence of an intrinsic length scale in a viscous fluid, swimmers have to limit their effectiveness to areas where they can directly interact with their paddles. A two-dimensional scallop consists of two parts that can move relative to each other with one degree of freedom, making this design suitable for investigation due to its simplicity. A two-dimensional scallop generates a net displacement over a 'kick cycle' when its internal degree of freedom is set to move in a specific way with its paddle within the body being stretched into an ellipse. However, when the shell is deformed into other non-circular shapes, there are points within the fluid that remain unchanged throughout the kick cycle, creating regions where the scallop can trap food particles for ingestion. A shape that optimizes the squared average distance between the scallop's mouth and its stomach results in a shape that resembles a heart, and this heart-shaped scallop can also achieve optimal displacement. Furthermore, when a particular type of hinge is used to limit the scallop's movement, there exists a unique shape that maximizes displacement, and this shape can be found using a combination of a finite

A significant decline in face-to-face social interactions in major cities during the COVID-19 pandemic has been observed, with the decrease in income diversity of social interactions in urban areas being more pronounced in comparison to other metrics. This significant decline was primarily driven by reduced social interactions between individuals from different backgrounds, with neighboring social interactions being less common among young people and women as a result. Government policies promoting social distancing were found to have different effects on social interaction diversity depending on whether they mandated staying at home or simply avoiding large gatherings. Research was conducted on 13 major cities globally, but the data was collected after the initial lockdown period. This study was pivotal in establishing baseline metrics for assessing the socioeconomic diversity of face-to-face social interactions, with implications for understanding human behavior and the spread of contagious diseases.

A new theory proposes that massive young stars, like Sh2-166, are formed from multiple mergers of smaller clumps of gas. However, it is unclear whether there is enough time for this process to occur before the star's structure is destroyed by energy released. Using simulations, researchers are examining the evolution of two closely situated gas clouds to determine the process of merging and its underlying physics. The simulations reveal that even when the energy released is great, it is confined to the outer layers of the clouds, preventing them from being destroyed. This process is further complicated by the presence of gas streams that are drawn towards the center by gravity. The streams may experience instabilities, which could lead to the release of energy in the form of jets. The results indicate that massive stars are formed through a process of merging that is governed by the balance between gravity and the central energy release, which is consistent with observations of outflows and gas that has been heated to great temperatures. This process is further supported by mass data obtained from observations of ionized gas, which indicate that massive stars are not accreting mass at a rate that would be expected if they were not formed through this process.

For a given mass and satisfying certain technical conditions, we've undertaken a key step in representing 2D wedge-local QFT in conformal gravity without a mass gap, by employing 4-100 times the natural scale as the cutoff. The procedure involves performing an integral over a wedge in the momentum space to modify the interaction endomorphisms of Longo-Witten in the Euclidean setting, resulting in approximations of wedge CFT that correspond to a net of Spohn's dynamics and contain essential features of 2D PTLF. These implemented endomorphisms yield a significant net of local elements within a wedge in the S-matrix state, with the condition of local equivalence to free fields maintained within a dense subset of the product of wedge elements.

This research focuses on assessing the mobile electromagnetic wave exposure that children, teenagers, schools, and hospitals may be subjected to from 5G cell towers. Unlike previous studies, a new approach is taken to estimate average exposure levels, which can be utilized in regulatory contexts to establish exposure limits around sensitive areas. By employing an open-source computational tool, we calculate how 5G cell towers' power is distributed and calculate the average exposure levels that children, teenagers, schools, and hospitals may be subjected to from 5G cell towers, which is crucial considering the widespread deployment of 5G technology.

This research paper develops a simplified Hamiltonian version of Dysthe's wave equation, accounting for water with constant circulation along its boundary. The equation is applicable to water currents that rotate in the same direction, and we demonstrate how a specific type of circulation can cause water waves to become unstable. Additionally, a connection is established between this modified Dysthe equation and a recently introduced model by El and Lake.

In this study, we develop a version of the Stokes formula for a specific type of integration measure, which is the image under a mapping from a locally convex space to another, and an operation known as the exterior derivative. Key elements include using the pull-back operation for exterior derivatives and a previously defined form of integration, denoted as $\int_{\Phi(M)}$, based on the properties of the locally convex space and the characteristics of the mapping $\Phi$.

This project presents a innovative sonar data integration method within a layered navigation framework using a Raspberry Pi 3 and eight sonar sensors. While operating on a Raspberry Pi presents performance constraints due to its limited CPU capabilities, this project successfully overcomes these limitations by developing a modular, layered control system that efficiently processes sonar data and generates precise navigation movements.

The proposed control algorithm features a unique approach to dealing with the non-linear nature of sonar measurements, allowing for a significant reduction in code complexity and memory usage. By breaking down the problem into smaller, linear components, each navigation module can be optimized for performance without compromising the overall system's efficiency.

The rapid dissemination of unverified news on social media poses significant challenges, making it crucial to develop effective methods for identifying false news. One method involves comparing generated overview texts with original articles to determine their authenticity. We explore three strategies to combine generated summaries with original texts for identifying false news, and these are evaluated through experiments. Our results show that comparing computed overview texts with original articles can effectively identify false news. Comparing generated summaries with original texts yields better results when using models specifically trained for text summarization rather than machine translation. Additionally, incorporating computational measures to compare sequences of original texts and their corresponding summaries enhances our fake news classification performance.

While observing a two-dimensional cross-section of a random field defined over a three-dimensional domain, we discover an intriguing phenomenon. As the point of observation moves outward in the radial direction, the average distance to the nearest point where the random field equals zero decreases, reminiscent of a bending effect. This phenomenon is then linked to an idealized physical model of a random string, governed by a one-dimensional Laplacian, subject to specific boundary conditions of zero points. We demonstrate that the average distance found empirically and theoretically aligns with this ratio in the radial direction.

This research paper proposes a novel decoding approach for Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) that utilizes an untrusted link. Traditionally, successive interference cancellation (SIC) is employed for signal decoding in NOMA systems, but it requires intricate and secure computations, making it an attractive target for attackers. To counter this, we introduce a decoding method called Successive Interference Decryption (SID), which relies on lighter-weight cryptographic techniques to decode signals. By analyzing SID, we explore various scenarios of successful attacks and develop criteria for its security. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of partial SID on decoding order and compare its performance with successive and linear interference cancellation methods. This research provides a foundation for implementing secure and efficient communications in Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOA) systems.

Inferring shape from contour is a challenging problem in shape analysis, an
intriguing application where internal structure information is unavailable.
When external information is limited, sparsity-based methods are particularly
useful due to their ability to provide interpretable results. Nevertheless,
standard $\ell_1$-norm PCA formulation is inapplicable in PCA's absence of
background information scenario. To rectify this issue, we introduce a
modified PCA formulation that incorporates the rotational invariance of
covariance into $\ell_1$-norm PCA. This new formulation is then used to
address shape analysis from contour by developing a corresponding objective
function. Next, a proximal gradient method is presented to efficiently solve
both $\ell_1$-norm PCA and shape analysis problems. This algorithm guarantees
convergence to an optimal solution at a linear rate. Experiments on synthetic
data and real contour information demonstrate the proposed method's
effectiveness and efficiency.

The rise of semantic annotation-based NLP applications has led to significant growth in Emotion-Related Question (ERQ) annotation. Open-emotion annotation, in particular, has seen substantial development. Although existing ERQ datasets are meticulously annotated, the increasing volume of data presents a laborious and costly process for further expansion. To promote the growth of ERQ datasets, a low-cost approach to accurately correcting their semantic annotations is proposed. Initially, a BERT-based automatic annotation method is introduced to produce rough annotations for unemotional questions, which are then used to correct the ERQ data's open-emotional annotations. The proposed correction approach is experimentally validated, and its effectiveness in accurately correcting ERQ annotations is demonstrated.

The research extends previous studies on energy contests to include totally ordered groups as a broader context. A key finding is that when the order group is the real numbers, there are infinitely many unique solution patterns for the contest, but in other order groups, the number of these solutions is limited and corresponds to the number of ways certain sequences can be arranged. Additionally, a specific subset of strategies, known as cyclic patterns, always results in a stable outcome, and these strategies are closely related to the structure of the order group through a concept called Hilbert's $k$-th closure.

Over the last decade, the study of pulsing polar stars has been hindered due to a lack of observations at the highest energy range in X-rays. This study aims to overcome this obstacle by utilizing the latest data from the Swift satellite, which allows for the examination of the relationship between the time variation of polar stars and their X-ray hardness states. We establish a set of selection criteria to identify the asynchronous and synchronous types of polar stars and analyze their spectral behavior. Our results show that the asynchronous polars experience more significant time variations in their X-ray hardness states compared to their synchronous counterparts. This study also provides a method for classifying the spectral states of polar stars based on their rotation periods and demonstrates the effectiveness of using Swift data to monitor these systems.

This study presents two distinct approaches for solving the time-dependent Reduced Basis approximation of Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems. Initially, we examine a monolithic method, where the Reduced Basis Approximation is applied to the combined fluid-structure domain and boundary. Subsequently, we explore a segmented approach, where the Reduction Technique is applied separately to the fluid and solid components. A key difference between these methods lies in how they handle the fluid-structure interface. In the monolithic approach, interface conditions are handled directly, whereas in the segmented approach, a coupling operator is employed to map the significantly smaller solid domain onto the larger fluid domain. This leads to a notable improvement in computational efficiency for the segmented approach. To further enhance performance, we also discuss a strategy that applies Reduction Technique only to a subset of degrees of freedom in the fluid domain, specifically those that significantly influence the solid domain. This method combines the advantages of both approaches, leading to substantial gains in efficiency without compromising accuracy.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate independently, they need an effective map representation that allows for efficient and intuitive movement. Current leading map representations, such as occupancy grids, have limitations when it comes to processing speed and scalability. A more intuitive and scalable approach is required for a robot to efficiently plan its path and move through unknown environments.

In this work, we present a novel, hierarchical topological diagram representation for navigation, which is designed to be both more human-like and suitable for robotic use. Our approach uses a compact, 2D 2D sketch to depict an environment, which is achieved through a grid-to-diagram conversion process that extracts key structural information. A hierarchical component is then added to capture local details that may be missed in the initial representation.

To test our diagram-based representation, we developed a neuro-symbolic navigation module that combines symbolic topological information with a visual understanding of the environment. Our results show that this approach outperforms previous sketch-based methods and allows for precise, efficient navigation in unknown environments.

Our proposed system, a joint effort by Indiana University and the University of Massachusetts Amherst, ranks second in this year's SemEval-2019 Task 6, which focuses on detecting aggressive language in social media posts. For predicting aggressive and non-aggressive posts, our system achieved an F-score of 0.823, while for detecting moderately aggressive language, it achieved an F-score of 0.721. We utilized a BERT-based model for initial predictions and refined those with a linear classifier, specifically an SVM, to identify moderately aggressive posts.

Researchers developed a sensitive method to detect minute changes in local magnetic fields by combining interferometry with an atom chip and exploiting the Meissner effect in a superconducting film. As a result, the phase shift detected was equivalent to roughly 0.02 pico-Tesla for a specific configuration of atoms and superconducting film, a precision that could be improved to around 0.005 pico-Tesla with potential technical advancements. This research also provides a theoretical framework for a new type of atomic magnetometer, offering a high precision and safety level free from potentially harmful laser light.

We investigate a novel magnetothermal proximity effect that arises from the interaction between a ferromagnetic material and a nonferromagnetic transition metal dichalcogenide with broken valley symmetry. This effect leads to the generation of spin-polarized heat currents in the TMD layer, and we find that it can be used to create a spin-dependent Seebeck voltage in response to a applied heat current, with the voltage being controllable through the magnetic anisotropy and exchange gap. By examining different interfaces and accounting for scattering processes, it is also possible to estimate the magnitude of this effect and apply it to the development of valley and thermal devices that utilize the valley-Pockels effect for low-power operation.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal effects influence gap-plasmon mode dynamics in parallel metallic surfaces as the gap between them narrows. By applying a nonlocal model, we determine the electric response at each point individually. In this model, the interaction within the gap leads to a spillover length that scales with the gap size, resulting in a distinct increase in mode decay rates and a reduction in their localization length to the order of the gap. This effect significantly impacts differences in electrochemical potential across nanostructures, with important implications for the performance of plasmonic devices and metamaterials, and paves the way for a practical design based on gap sizes on the order of 10 nanometers. Our theoretical predictions are verified through numerical simulations using a two-length-scale model and a time-dependent simulation of electrons within the gap.

A robust normalization process is examined for the Calculus of Constructions, 
in which Inductive Families are included, specifically addressing the problem of 
non-terminating reduction in the main system through a stratified $\beta$-reduction 
in the sub-system. This increase in robustness is achieved even when the sub-system 
contains multiple types capable of encoding natural numbers.

We've created an educational framework for understanding the 1D Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model's physics by using visual aids and interactive tools. 
This framework simplifies the typically advanced concepts associated with many-body Hamiltonians, topological Hamiltonians, and band theory. 
It allows for a clear understanding of the SSH model's topology via the winding number, which can be viewed both numerically and analytically. 
Moreover, the framework explores the impact of introducing an electric field on the system's charge phases through the use of Harper's equation. 
It also investigates the exchange of edge states when non-identical SSH chains are joined, thereby exchanging their topological characteristics. 
This exchange can be understood through the use of effective dimer models. 
Additionally, it introduces a topological invariant known as the polarization difference, offering an alternative topological descriptor. 
This framework can be further utilized to understand more complex variants of the SSH model.

This paper provides a novel, geometric perspective on finite Gaussian and elliptical Gaussian mixture models using stochastic convex geometry. It then leverages this new perspective to offer an intuitive proof of the capacity limit for these types of high-dimensional models.

To examine two-loop supergravity within the context of N=4 super Yang-Mills on AdC5 x S5, we construct an on-shell action that incorporates two-loop vertex and tree-level four-line interactions within a supergravity background. By leveraging large N and low energy approximations, we derive the beta function at the two-loop supergravity level, finding agreement with field theory predictions up to the critical four-loop level in supergravity. Furthermore, by isolating specific four-line interaction components in the supergravity spectrum, we establish a relationship between these interactions and the corresponding two-loop field theory contributions.

High-performance computing on GPUs is being hindered by limited memory and inadequate data structures for efficiently processing complex, real-world data.
Existing GPU memory management techniques, such as memory pools, are constrained by their sequential nature and inability to handle dynamic memory requirements.
We have developed a parallel dynamic memory allocator called DynaSOAr on GPUs, which overcomes these limitations by allowing arbitrary, non-contiguous memory allocations.
DynaSOAr utilizes parallel algorithms to create an object-oriented interface that is both flexible and adaptable to different memory scenarios.
We have demonstrated that custom data structures can be optimized for better data locality and overall performance.
However, this approach requires a significant investment of time and expertise, which is not always feasible.
As a result, we have created a high-level interface that simplifies the development process while retaining the performance benefits of carefully designed data structures.

This paper establishes sufficient conditions for a linear operator to have a sublinear counterpart that retains the same boundedness properties on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. We also examine the boundedness of composition operators on these spaces, obtaining a similar condition for their linear and sublinear counterparts. Additionally, we assess the boundedness of commutators involving linear operators and test functions on generalized mixed Morrey spaces, obtaining a relevant criterion.

We develop a comprehensive method that seamlessly integrates relative theories of electrons with advanced models for magnetic impurities, enabling the prediction of magnetic moments and magnetic anisotropy energy in various Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states. This methodology is applied to examine a single Mn atom and clusters consisting of one to five Mn atoms on the surface of Niobium, specifically in the (110) plane. Our analysis is based on full-potential methods that account for the complex interactions of electrons, including their spin-orbit effects. Our findings show that a single Mn atom produces an ISR state with magnetic moments oriented perpendicular to that of the substrate. In contrast, linear and triangular pairs and clusters of Mn atoms produce MSR states with magnetic moments aligned in the same direction as the Nb atoms' moments. Lateral pairs of Mn atoms also exhibit ISR states for those configurations located on the narrowest parts of the Nb atomic grooves. Furthermore, we observe a significant variation in the magnitude of the magnetic moments of both ISR and MSR states as they increase in size.

Our proposed FourierMask is an instance segmentation method that utilizes implicit neural representations and a Fourier-based mask. By encoding a 2D mask as a parametric function, FourierMask maps this parameter to an instance's mask through a learned transformation. The mask parameters can be provided in various formats, such as angles or pixel coordinates. Our model is composed of two parts: a base network that encodes input data and a Fourier-based mask network. The mask network is simplified to only two layers, with the mask network being activated by the difference between the code produced by the base network and a learned reference code. Only the mask network needs to be specific to the instance, making it an efficient design. Our method outperforms current instance segmentation methods using implicit representations by a significant margin, achieving an improvement of 20% in performance. Additionally, our network can be easily integrated with any basic encoding network, such as CM3, without affecting its performance. The FourierMask design is a robust and versatile instance segmentation method.

All previously verified cases of the double characterization theorem for topological immersions into graphs have only considered cases where the source space is connected. This article will fully describe the possible topological structures of one-dimensional sources under immersions into graphs, and completely prove a theorem that any such connected graph can be immised into a source space that is composed of two separate pieces.

Current satellite-derived cloud properties rely on passive optical measurements, which are limited to analyzing transparent clouds. Approximately half of the global cloud cover is too opaque for light to penetrate, hindering our understanding of thick convective clouds' internal structure. This study presents a novel approach to determining the virtual particle size at the center of opaque convective clouds by leveraging data from the MISR and MODIS satellite instruments. Our analysis reveals a consistent pattern in the loci of virtual particle size, which holds true across different locations and seasons. This method is then applied to identify the characteristics of large, opaque convective clouds in southwestern North America during the warm season.

We examine the impact of a time-varying magnetic field on an plasma slab that undergoes relativistic self-induced transparency. By utilizing an analytic solution for this scenario, we assess how the temporal changes in RIT affect both reflection of the laser and related ion acceleration. Our findings suggest that choosing an appropriate peak frequency and self-consistent parameters can enhance both the energy and distance ions travel. In addition, both simulations and theoretical models in this study align with each other.

The TESS mission has significantly expanded our knowledge of exoplanets by identifying numerous candidates within the nearby stars, which are often observed across the full electromagnetic spectrum. TESS detects planets in a wide range of sizes and types, ranging from Earth-sized to Jupiter-sized, obviating the need to rely solely on its data to study the full range of transiting exoplanets. Combining TESS photometry with ground-based observations of stellar activity and bulk properties, we can significantly enhance our detection capabilities and, in some cases, determine the physical properties of numerous additional exoplanets. In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of the TESS system TOI-712, which consists of three transiting mini-Neptunes orbiting an early K-type star. By merging TESS data with ground-based astrometry, we were able to refine the astrometric measurements and derive a precise stellar radius of 0.745 R⊙. Additionally, we determined the age of the system to be approximately 600 million years, and discovered that the inner two planets TOI-712 b and c exhibit orbital resonances with a 3:2 ratio. By merging TESS data with ground-based spectroscopy, we were able to determine the stellar parameters and derive the masses, radii, and temperatures of all three planets. Notably, TOI-712 c has a minimum mass of 0.071 M

This paper presents a first-principles investigation of possible applications of carbon and nitrogen doped TiO2 in creating electronic devices. Using the rutile TiO2 as a model, we explored N-type TiO2 and examined its structure, electronic behavior, and magnetic properties. We used the PBE0 method to accurately assess the effects of self-interaction on charge localization. N-doping was found to create a localized state within the band gap of TiO2, and this state's energy can be altered by adjusting the PBE0 mixing percentage. Additionally, we observed that spin-polarized states are created near the valence band edge due to electron repulsion, and the strength of this polarization can be controlled by modifying the PBE0 mixing percentage, offering a potential application for realising quantum states in oxide materials.

The primary characteristics of top quarks remain relatively unknown. Due to the limited data available, current constraints on their nature are heavily influenced by theoretical assumptions. To overcome this, a new analysis method called Elastic Energy is introduced, which allows for the discovery of unique properties of top quarks. This approach takes advantage of the specific signature of top quark pairs produced through recoil reactions. Because this process is difficult to generate, it results in both top quarks retaining much of their initial energy. Consequently, it enables the measurement of several unique properties of top quarks that cannot be obtained from traditional methods. Although the rate of this reaction is low, it can be increased by utilizing specialized processes that focus on the production of top quarks when gluons are scattered off quarks. Despite being suppressed, this process can still result in a significant number of events that can be detected. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this new method, concrete examples of unique searches for first-generation fermions, quark compositeness, and supersymmetry are provided.

The proposed technique for analyzing the intra-cluster medium turbulence relies on measuring the second-order structure functions of bright features in X-rays. However, due to the complex nature of this problem, deconvolving radial profiles to obtain a turbulence measurement introduces ambiguities in profile comparisons that need to be addressed. This study focuses on resolving these issues by limiting the analysis to regions with uniform physical properties and assessing the accuracy of different profile-fitting methods. Different fitting approaches were tested to determine their impact on measurement accuracy. It was found that fitting the logarithm of intensity using appropriate statistical distribution functions, specifically a Gaussian and Rayleigh distribution, resulted in the lowest ambiguity in measurements. Furthermore, it was discovered that even simple linear fitting produced comparable turbulence values, indicating that the method is relatively robust to the choice of profile-fitting function. The study also explored how fitting errors and measurement uncertainties affect the accuracy of turbulence estimates and found that high-quality, smooth profiles with low measurement uncertainties allowed for precise turbulence estimates. In contrast, noisy profiles with high measurement uncertainties led to inflated turbulence values. It was concluded that accurate turbulence measurements should be limited to profiles with low ambiguity, high smoothness, and low measurement uncertainties.

The concept of Ramsey upper richness for graph properties was initially proposed and analyzed by Montelstra and Seiverly in 2008. They defined it as the minimum number k for an n vertex graph, where any edge coloring using k colors using graph property P will result in at least one color appearing as a large subgraph. Currently, there is no established method to determine the Ramsey upper richness for infinite graph properties with vertex transitivity. In this study, we prove that the lower bound for the Ramsey upper richness of the triangle-free property in infinite graph properties with vertex transitivity, that is, at least two, and for any graph property P that includes being a triangle, the lower bound for the Ramsey upper richness is at least K.

We developed a novel statistical method to study the anisotropic behavior of structures within the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) in our Galaxy's bulge. This method involves using two-dimensional correlations to examine the anisotropic properties of molecular gas within the CMZ, which we observed using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). As the highest density region in the Galactic disk, the CMZ is heavily influenced by gravitational forces and the central supermassive black hole, making it crucial for understanding star and galaxy formation. However, current models lack ANISOTROPIC resolution. By applying ALMA's high sensitivity and precision, we discovered significant anisotropic variations in gas densities within the CMZ when studied using two-dimensional correlations. These variations, which are not fully accounted for in existing models, are crucial for a comprehensive understanding of the CMZ and its role in star and galaxy formation.

A sudden onset of Bell's palsy is commonly identified through the observation of eye asymmetry in a video. To meet this requirement, our proposed system is centered on detecting eye anomalies by processing videos at a per-eye level. Firstly, color is removed from the video to eliminate skin tone bias. Moreover, to prevent errors caused by variations in head position and facial angles, we establish a reference line that aligns with the nose and eye. To do this, we employ a combination of eye-in-head coordinate transformation and feature point matching. Moreover, to ensure the reliability of our method, it is validated on a dataset comprising 1000 videos of people with normal eyes and those affected by Bell's palsy. Experimental results show that our proposed method successfully distinguishes between normal eyes and those affected by Bell's palsy in 99% of cases. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in real-world applications, it is being tested on videos obtained from YouTube.

Our research focuses on quantifying the impact of noise in the dynamic vector space when modeling scatchard-qed using qutrits to represent fields and link interactions. We will introduce time-dependent error metrics to evaluate the simulation's inaccuracy and smoothness, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of the qudit's dimension, the pattern of noise, and the system's field. We will also explore how to mitigate noise through error correction, particularly in the GKP encoding scheme, and demonstrate the impact of dynamic errors on system equilibrium and scattering patterns.

In the non-relativistic regime, we propose using metal film targets to enhance the generation of spin-polarized e+ by a 100 GW laser. The targets are pre-treated with short laser pulses to increase the number of inner-shell Ag-3d electrons interacting with the main pulse, which significantly improves the $\sigma$ asymmetry of 10.5-% $\sigma$-polarized e+. In contrast, the 2.5-% $\sigma$ asymmetry of 10 MeV e+ generated by irradiating Cu-films with 1.5 TW pulses is reported in the QED regime.

A subgroup of a group G is considered wide if it intersects deeply with the subgraph of G generated by its elements. We have discovered that all finite special linear groups, along with their torsion-free versions, contain wide subgroups. Conversely, in a significantly larger class of finite groups, specifically those that are not in the A-series, we have found that there are many instances of especially deep wide subgroups.

This study presents an innovative low-power voltage circuit designed to measure temperature with remarkable precision and efficiency. Unlike traditional approaches, this compact detector circumvents the need for a microcontroller or temperature-to-digital conversion by directly generating a unique voltage corresponding to the current temperature. This low-power design is particularly well-suited for applications in wearable technology, mobile devices, and the Internet of Things, where minimizing power consumption is critical. The detector's performance was tested over a broad temperature range, and it was found to achieve exceptional accuracy and resolution with minimal energy usage per conversion.

We analyzed the long-term stability of magnetized stars with axial symmetry under a rotating frame of reference. By applying a method called 'normal mode analysis', we investigated whether certain magnetic force configurations maintain their equilibrium over time. Our study revealed that these forces become unstable when their forces are transformed through a specific mathematical operation twice, indicating the presence of wave-like behavior. This threshold was found to be closely associated with the frequency of the resulting forces, confirming that magnetic configurations in magnetic stars with axial symmetry are generally unstable.

We test nonperturbative techniques in quantum field theory, specifically dual gradient flow, to study the evolution of effective actions as auxiliary variables flow. Our focus is on obtaining and analyzing the phase structure of $N$-component $O(N)$ models in one-dimensional space by examining the probability distribution of field configurations' center-of-mass modes under a given scale. We present results from simulations of $N$-component models for $N$ values of 0.5, 3, 80, and 120, and observe that the critical values of an SUSY partner field vary in a way that can be  described by a universal scaling function of $1/N$. We also find that the dual gradient flow can accurately represent the universal long-distance behavior of the model, as shown by the results of the computed distribution of center-of-mass modes.

We present Pied Piper, a 3D music visualization experience for VR that utilizes
point clouds. Unlike traditional 3D models, virtual reality users can interact with
their own audio in a unique and intuitive manner. With simple controls, users can
manipulate various visual aspects, creating an engaging and personalized experience
that blends visual and auditory elements for optimal impact in virtual reality.

This work offers a comprehensive update to recent advancements in constructing various differential structures on Lie groupoids and stacks. We aim to explain several concepts, including multivector fields, differential forms, vector bundles, torsion one-forms, and canonical connections, from the perspective of a underlying Lie groupoid. Additionally, we seek to illuminate a key property of a constructed object on a Lie groupoid $\mathcal{G}$, which arises when a corresponding structure on the base manifold $M$ is equipped with specific properties. We aim to illustrate a key principle that the constructed objects on Lie groupoids and stacks can be viewed as enhancements of their counterparts on the base manifold, characterized by an exactness property that reflects the deeper relationship between a Lie groupoid and its associated stack.

Researchers have identified an unusual feature in the Dragon infrared dark cloud, a dense region of space where stars are born. They discovered a spherical area in the center of the Dragon, which is expanding rapidly at about 1.4 kilometers per second. This area has a mass of 1.4 million times that of our sun and is located in a region known for forming massive stars. Studies comparing similar regions in another star-forming area, called Ophiuchus, have revealed a similar pattern of expansion in their core regions. This discovery provides valuable insights into the process of massive star formation by highlighting how core regions may create favorable conditions for star formation through their dynamic movements.

Godel modal logics can be viewed as extensions of basic propositional logic that utilize accessibility relations. This basic understanding is expanded upon in this study, which classifies algebraic and relational frameworks for a broader range of logic systems, including many with T and N axioms, over multiple domains. Key algebraic models for these logic systems were developed in the latter half of the 20th century, but this study focuses on their relational counterparts. Although some algebraic models offered insights into proof-theoretic properties, they often lacked intuitive algebraic models due to the complex T and N operators used. To address this challenge, this study specifically targets an algebraic model for the S4.3 paracomplete logic system.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable data for understanding the spatial layout of environments, which can be leveraged by both humans and machines to improve navigation and identification of ways for robots and vehicles. This tutorial explores various aspects of LiDAR technology and its data, introducing fundamental concepts of machine intelligence using 3D point clouds. It covers classification methods, convolutional neural network applications on 3D data, and benchmark datasets for evaluating performance. Additionally, it introduces advanced topics such as segmenting self-driving cars and establishing 3D scene graphs. This material is designed to be accessible to beginners and provide insights for more experienced researchers in machine learning with LiDAR 3D point clouds.

We examine a random dynamic system on the surface of a sphere and a positive-definite matrix, then prove the existence of a specific probability distribution that remains unchanged over time. We also demonstrate that, for many cases, this distribution can be represented as a sum of two independent components. We further investigate the asymptotic behavior of the system's law as the rate of change in the random dynamic system on the sphere increases, demonstrating that it converges to the uniform distribution on the sphere's surface. We also establish that itex$ t \mapsto \Phi(X_t) $ is a martingale, where $ X $ is a reference process that behaves similarly to the dynamic system and $ \operatorname{law}(X_\infty) $ has compact support. We also provide examples of how these results can be applied to understand the long-term behavior of random dynamic systems.

Our research employs machine learning-based multivariate analysis to delve into the spatial correlation of neutrino arrival directions and overhead cosmic ray spectra, aligned to sub-degree precision, to pinpoint possible cosmic ray sources. This method complements existing studies on the separation between neutrinos and cosmic rays at various energy levels. We directly compare the observed data to neutrino and independent cosmic ray simulations, focusing on the score distribution around the highest energy cosmic ray locations. The observed alignment between neutrinos and cosmic rays can't rule out the idea that at least some of the cosmic ray sources are at least as distant as the closest identified cosmic ray sources.

The friction between surfaces in liquid foams mimicking granular materials diverges from classical predictions due to their unique internal structure. This study investigates the root cause of this discrepancy by exploring the contact line structure and interfacial tension in two-dimensional water foams made of SDS. Our findings reveal an unexpectedly long contact line structure and an unexpectedly short length scale for capillary interfacial tension, with the former significantly larger than the foam's mean free path. This large contact line structure is found to directly correlate with the elevated friction observed in liquid foams.

This research focuses on classifying nine types of skin cancer and a benign condition called nevus, using an efficient method to reduce data variability. We propose a two-step approach to pre-process images and minimize distortions caused by image capture techniques. Initially, we applied two different processing steps to the dataset and used entropy to identify and remove outlier samples that do not accurately represent the category they belong to. A final skin cancer diagnosis was performed using a convolutional neural network after removing the identified outlier samples. This approach was used to determine the presence of a particular type of cancer in a dataset containing images of all eight categories plus nevus.

We're studying a complex phenomenon known as Hele-Shaw hydrophobic instability, specifically how it interacts with rotation in multiple directions. Using flexible fingers as a means of accommodation, we observe that the finger state adapts to changes in the rotating environment. As the rate of rotation increases, the finger state shifts from being flat to curved, and even flips over at certain points. The shape of the curved fingers is influenced by the ratio of rotation to pressure difference, and the transition points are explained by analyzing the balance of forces at play. Our work fills in knowledge gaps about the hydrophobic effect in rotating systems and provides valuable insights for the design of microfluidic devices and fluid-based measurement tools that rely on wetted bearings.

The mixing volume change hypothesis underlies the statistical interpretation of entropy, yet contradicts thermodynamic principles.  Our research diverges from conventional understanding by proposing that entropy change should be measured only within consistent thermodynamic states.  We outline a two-step procedure to connect initial and final states through states that maintain pressure and external volume equilibrium.  We demonstrate that this approach successfully predicts entropy changes during volume alterations, including the surprising finding that mixing results in increased entropy due to distinct particle labeling effects.  We also successfully apply the microcanonical method to verify our proposed framework.

A cycle alkyne molecule, specifically 1-ethynyl-2,3-dihydrocyclopenta-2,4-diene, has been identified in the interstellar space for the first time. This discovery was made using observations from the IRAM 30m telescope and the NOEMA telescope array, which detected two closely related molecules as faint spectral signals. These molecules are TMC-1 ethynyl cyclopentadiene isotopologues, distinguished by the substitution of a terminal carbon atom in the CCH and CN forms of the molecules with N. Based on analysis of the spectral data, the concentration of both TMC-1 cycloalkyne and the two ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecules was calculated. Surprisingly, cycle unsaturated molecules in this area are found to be more abundant than their linear counterparts. When taking into account previous underestimations of some cycle alkyne concentrations, it appears that linear and cyclic unsaturated molecules are roughly equally abundant in TMC-1.

In neural machine translation, current models that use whole-target attention face issues generating inaccurate predictions due to including previously generated words in the attention mechanism. To address this, an alternative approach using self-attention has been proposed, but it risks generating redundant information. To tackle this issue, an innovative approach called Look-ahead Focus (Lf) was introduced, which forces the model to focus on previously generated words while self-attention is applied to the entire target sequence. By applying this approach at each decoding step, a more targeted selection is made of the most relevant past outputs. Lf can be viewed as a way to apply Tries to the non-causal attention model, and experimental results show significant improvements in metrics such as Perplexity, BLEU, and F1 scores when compared to traditional causal attention and self-attention methods.

A translation analogy is used to explain the intricate nature of a technical grid architecture, which can be compared to a language that is difficult for outsiders to grasp. However, much like a skilled translator, a key individual can simplify the grid for external developers and facilitate their ability to create applications that are compatible with the grid architecture. A translation-focused methodology is demonstrated to be a driving force in advancing the grid computing system, which is similar to how the work of Gerardus Douen and his team significantly contributed to the grid's development and functionality.

In the context of Unified Dark Matter (UDM), researchers have developed a specific model that incorporates a specific dissipation mechanism, drawing on a previously established prototype. By applying a dissipation mechanism to a specific potential, they have derived the corresponding friction term and rate, and then used this to modify the Barotropic Fluid Equation of State (EFE) with an additional term. Through this process, they have deduced the Hubble parameter, density, and deceleration rate, and then compared their redshift-dependent predictions to existing observational data. Notably, their model's predictions for the density and deceleration rate show significant improvement, and they have also found that a specific dark energy model with dissipation can potentially avoid the Big Rip scenario in the future.

To deepen our understanding of curiosity in learners, a new multimodal approach is proposed that integrates physiological and self-reported data. Current methods relying solely on self-reporting have limitations in accurately capturing curiosity's complex nature. A literature review highlights the need to examine curiosity's dynamic fluctuations in a learning context. Although self-reporting remains a key component, the added inclusion of physiological data has the potential to provide a more comprehensive understanding of curiosity's nuances. This study aims to pilot a new approach that analyzes curiosity's dynamic changes in a small group of engineering students during a hands-on learning session. Combining self-reporting and physiological measurements, such as skin conductance, will allow for a more detailed understanding of curiosity's dynamic fluctuations, potentially revealing unreported methods through advanced data analysis.

Spatial statistical modeling often incorporates correlation structures based on a given metric, like the Euclidean distance, but this approach can be computationally expensive and lacks flexibility for adapting to complex domains. A more adaptable alternative is using a stationary covariance model based on a graph, where node connections are defined by a binary adjacency matrix. Such a model provides a simple and efficient way to generate realizations of random fields over large datasets, while also being easily adaptable to novel datasets. Building on this, we introduce a graph-based Mat\'ern model that combines simplicity with a useful connection to an underlying random process, while ensuring positive definiteness for any graph. This model is further developed with a drift component, which allows for more accurate modeling of trends and smooth variations in the data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a range of computational experiments and real-world applications, including adaptive sampling, model fitting, and data reconstruction.

Urban road networks are complex and highly interconnected systems that can be effectively monitored using a new approach leveraging large numbers of ridesourcing vehicles. By applying graph theory and statistical methods, we've developed a framework to identify hidden road segments from cell phone data, determining the most sensitive missing edges and providing a robust approach to reconstructing the complete network from a partially observed system. Our method is interpreted through a statistical lens and validated with real-world data from Chicago, Chicago and Los Angeles, showcasing its efficiency and capability to detect nearly all road segments.

Neutrino effects can be studied through $J/\psi$ decay into $\gamma$ plus anything, and by setting limits on this process we gain insight into new physics that could be represented by effective field theories. By analyzing these theories at the JLab, Jefferson Lab, we can study initial state radiative neutrino interactions, particularly $\nu_\mu I^+ \to \mu^+ \bar{\nu}_\mu \gamma$. If the coefficient for this interaction is within the range of 1 to 100, JLab would be able to detect neutrino-induced events. Additionally, the same theoretical framework can be applied to dark matter searches involving invisible $J/\psi$ decays. Under similar assumptions, the Jefferson Lab facilities would be able to detect dark matter with masses between 0.1 and 1 GeV with cross sections as low as $10^{-36}$ cm$^2$.

We have developed variable stepsize self-decomposing linear implicit multistep implicit methods for efficiently solving standard differential equations. These methods maintain order reduction properties even when the stepsize changes, and we have derived conditions for them to be statistically stable. Some variable stepsize methods have been constructed and their global accuracy verified through numerical experiments.

Our work extends the functional singular spectrum analysis to higher-dimensional functional time series, using a spectral approach. A key result shows that a multivariate functional SSA accurately reconstructs the underlying functional time series with a convergence rate of n^(2/5).

Recent research indicates that Automated Speech Emotion Recognition (ASER) performance tends to be significantly better when emotions are categorized into more fine-grained classes, yet the majority of ASER systems exhibit a consistent bias towards predicting these more numerous classes. This results in most users receiving predictions for the less frequent emotion classes with a much lower accuracy. In this paper, we investigate this issue of prediction bias by introducing two key concepts: overstable and overreactive models. We argue that most ASER systems are subject to the detrimental effects of both overstable and overreactive models, leading to high accuracy on training data but poor generalization. Specifically, we find that (1) most data sets used for Emotion Recognition contain a significant amount of label noise, leading to models that overstable on these noisy labels; and (2 most ASER models exhibit significant performance drops when tested on label-cleaned versions of these data sets, indicating that these models are overreactive. To address these issues, we propose a straightforward yet effective approach to address both overstable and overreactive models. Our method successfully addresses the predictive bias issue, leading to more balanced predictions across all emotion classes. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reducing prediction bias across multiple data sets and emotion categories.

The overall persistence of one-dimensional random walks is typically studied through various approaches, and recently, a new concept called local time persistence was introduced for random walks in 1 dimension. This new idea measures the duration it takes for a random walk to visit specific points and has demonstrated a global persistence pattern. However, the probability of persistent behavior in this context does not always follow a power law pattern, and for cases where the dimension is two dimensions or less, the persistent probability is found to be constant regardless of the time period. Although this finding seems counterintuitive given the constant spatial distribution, it is worth noting that the concept of local time persistence differs from traditional persistent concepts due to the concentrated nature of random walks at particular points in time. The research presented here aims to establish global persistence patterns for one and two-dimensional random walks in these contexts.

A plasma characterization has been performed to verify the helicon mode of the IShTAR plasma source, which is part of an ion source test facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics.  The source, which has been recently upgraded, allows for the plasma discharge in multiple modes including helicon.  In this helicon mode, a closed magnetic field configuration is created to enhance plasma discharge and increase the plasma density.  In order to obtain the helicon mode, specific ratios between the plasma discharge parameters must be met.  The upgraded source features improved power coupling and greater flexibility in adjusting the source parameters.  A plasma density measurement was made using interferometry and compared to a continuity equation calculation, which relies on discharge current, electron temperature, electron attachment and ionization rates, as well as ion diffusion.  The agreement between these two plasma density calculations in helicon mode confirms the model's correctness.  However, there are discrepancies in non-helicon modes due to non-classical ion diffusion.  The control of the source in helicon mode allows for a plasma density that meets the requirements for neutral beam neutralization in a compact configuration and with better control over the neutral beam energy distribution.

To control an undesirable species, introducing a microbial pesticide that targets the species and is non-harmful to other organisms is a viable option. A modified predator-prey model incorporating this strategy was analyzed mathematically, including a carrier-free subsystem whose equilibrium point was studied for stability using a linearization method. A global stability theorem was established using a Lyapunov function, and the carrier-free system's dynamics were simulated. A carrier-dependent system was then simulated to determine parameter values that ensure the system's persistence, ultimately demonstrating the effectiveness of this control method in theory.

To accurately diagnose cancer, a pathologist must analyze histopathology images and identify nuclei within the sample. This task is extremely time-consuming and complex, making it an ideal candidate for automation through computer-aided diagnosis systems. While previous studies have successfully developed such systems, they often rely on extracting features using labor-intensive methods like patch segmentation and background removal. In contrast, a histopathology image contains numerous overlapping nuclei, rendering feature extraction from raw images an infeasible approach for deep learning models. In response, a two-stage system called W-Net has been proposed, which utilizes a deep learning model to directly classify non-cancerous, cancerous, and background areas from processed images. This system leverages digital image processing techniques to generate more informative and efficient feature representations, which in turn allow for a reduction in the number of network layers and overall computational cost. As a result, the network can effectively learn from the extracted features and achieve a balance between performance and efficiency.

For a prime $p$ and an integer $n \geq 1$, let $\Omega_n$ be the set of non-singular skew-symmetric matrices of size $n$ over the field of $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Z}_p$, and $\operatorname{O}(\Omega_n)$ the set of odd special orthogonal matrices that preserve $\Omega_n$. This work proves the local exchange theorem for the Hecke operator acting on the representation function of the group $\operatorname{O}(\Omega_n)$ for primes $p$ not dividing $n$ and the index $|\operatorname{Sp}_{2p}(2)|$. Consequently, it establishes the local equidistribution theorem for the local representation function of $\operatorname{O}(\Omega_n)$ under the Hecke operator acting on $\operatorname{Sp}_{2p}(2)$ for the set of primes not dividing $n$ and applying Baggett's equidistribution criterion, it shows that $\operatorname{O}(\Omega_n)$ satisfies the local Hecke equidistribution property with respect to the set of primes not dividing $n$ and the index $|\operatorname{Sp}_{2p}(2)|$.

Ribenboim and Zohar introduced two novel graph theory concepts: a graph G is considered to be on a hamiltonian path index if it has a (n-1)-spanning directed graph, and one with a hamiltonian path in its line graph is called line hamiltonian path. This research paper proves that graphs with line hamiltonian paths are those that are line traceable, and it provides a criterion for hamiltonian path in 2k-line graphs. Furthermore, it offers a condition for 2k-line graphs to be line hamiltonian path.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, triggered by SARS-CoV-2, can cause a build-up of this type of cell death which, if unchecked, leads to more severe symptoms and higher mortality rates.  Our analysis of a single-cell model reveals that factors such as the level of PAMPs detected by the cell, the speed at which PAMPs are cleared, and the effects of inflammatory blockers on cell behavior play key roles in determining the outcome of pyroptosis.  Changes in these factors can lead to more severe cell death or stabilize the system to prevent an increase in PAMP levels.  However, it was found that cells with a high sensitivity to PAMPs lead to uncontrolled cell death regardless of the application of inflammatory blockers.  These findings provide valuable insights for designing better cell therapies and cell death management strategies.

We investigate the problem of learning optimal policies in Markov decision processes where agents lack awareness of some key state variables that significantly impact rewards. This problem is analogous to reinforcement learning with passive observation. Under certain conditions, agents can successfully learn optimal policies despite only receiving partial and indirect feedback. However, in most scenarios, the agents' reward information is limited, severely hindering their learning capabilities. This research reveals a fundamental limitation on how quickly optimal policies can be learned within reasonable time frames. Furthermore, we explore strategies to accelerate the learning process by allowing the agents to actively gather information through additional actions and by developing a novel approach to remove irrelevant state variables and rewards that agents cannot observe or experience directly. We validate our method by applying it to both simple test cases and complex robotic applications involving a quadrotor and a quadrupedal robot in reinforcement learning environments.

We introduce HELMHOLTZ, a new validator for Tezos smart contracts that is based on refinement types and automated theorem proving. Contrary to existing approaches, our use of refinement types allows us to specify postconditions for refinement, enabling the definition of desired system behaviors in contracts. Our approach is novel in several aspects: it is the first to apply automated theorem proving and refinement types to the validation of Tezos smart contracts, and it provides a richer semantic framework for validating contracts. Our method is based on Michail, a backend written in Coq that supports a substantial subset of OCaml. Our framework's capabilities are demonstrated through the validation of multiple Tezos contracts, including a safe transfer operation in UTR, a complex interest rate calculation in BAKA, and the sophisticated treasury management protocol in the Tezos Treasury Protocol.

Due to their effectiveness in extracting relevant information, convolutional neural networks and their derivatives, like Graph Convolutional Neural Networks, rely on the concept of matched filtering for feature extraction. Although GCNs have been highly successful, the underlying theory of their operation remains unclear. This research explores the connectedness of matched filtering to the fundamental principles of GCNs, demonstrating that many characteristics of graph signals can be utilized to interpret the matched filtering process in this context. Furthermore, it is proposed that the graph Fourier transform, a generalization of the conventional Fourier transform, provides a more comprehensive understanding of GCNs. Based on this, the research introduces a basic GCN model and utilizes mathematical methods to explain its behavior, including the application of matched filtering and group algebra. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the graph convolution can be interpreted as a low-pass filter operation, similar to the conventional signal processing approach.

Starting with a specific 2+1 dimensional gravity theory that includes a scalar field, we identify a set of static solutions composed of interlocking vortices and require the theory to admit these solutions. By restricting the theory to certain fields and making certain restrictions, we find that it can be described by a Chern-Simons form. However, this description only applies if certain constraints are met on the remaining fields. A Chern-Simons form exists with significantly fewer constraints, allowing us to find solutions using the equations of a topological field theory. These solutions include static configurations as well as black holes with specific properties. Additionally, we find that rotating black holes with complex structures can be transformed into static configurations through a specific process, known as the Melvin twist.

We've analyzed the properties of D-branes in theories of $N=4$ super Yang-Mills, finding that non-unitary symmetry transformations can be represented through Lagrangian formulations. This discovery allows for the extension of non-unitary symmetry to include branes, confirming its invariance under the action of these transformations. Furthermore, we observe that when odd numbers of M5-branes are present, the global symmetry on their worldvolume includes a non-unitary component, which is conserved through the action of these transformations.

One challenging aspect in strain-based elastography is accurately determining the lateral shift of ultrasound signals. Traditional methods face difficulties due to sub-sample precision limitations and edge effects that arise from the scanning pattern of conventional ultrasound arrays. These issues become even more pronounced in Synthetic Aperture Elastography (SAE) due to the SA acquisition method. This study introduces a synthetic aperture technique called Virtual Source SA (VS-SAE) that overcomes these limitations. In VS-SAE, a synthetic aperture is created by combining SAE strain images, effectively making it appear as though a single VS transducer is sending and receiving pulses. This allows for precise strain estimation in areas near the sample's edges through post-processing. A high-resolution SA SAE system based on this virtual transducer technique was developed and demonstrated to yield accurate, high-resolution strain and displacement maps using high-frequency (15 MHz) ultrasound in gel phantoms under compression. The results showed that the VS-SAE method provided robust, precise displacement and strain measurements, particularly near the sample's edges, outperforming conventional SAE methods.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in utilizing the programming language Prolog for specifying and verifying algorithms, as it allows for a seamless integration of algorithms with logical proofs. This approach, known as Logical Pseudocode, builds upon the foundation of Prolog by introducing features such as bidirectional rules and logical disjunctions, which are absent in traditional Prolog. We have developed an extended Prolog dialect that encompasses these additional features and can be used to verify algorithms through a sound interpretation into first-order logic. We have demonstrated the efficacy of Logical Pseudocode by specifying and validating an all-shortest-paths algorithm, also known as Bellman-Ford, and by introducing a sound and complete method for interpreting these specifications, based on a step-by-step execution semantics.

The notion of Boolean lattice $\mathcal{B}_n$ is a directed acyclic graph composed of binary vectors of length $n$, with an edge from binary vector $x$ to binary vector $y$ if $x$ is less than or equal to $y$ under a specific binary comparison. Researchers are currently exploring $\mathcal{B}_n$'s combinatorial properties by randomly permuting binary vectors to create an random Boolean lattice $\mathcal{Q}_n$. In this study, we establish the existence of a sufficiently large subset $C$ within $\mathcal{Q}_n$ such that the directed edges of the subgraph formed by $C$ in the Boolean lattice can be colored to create an embedding of a poset $P$ in the resulting two-colored subgraph. We prove that certain antichains and star-like posets allow for this embedding, but embedding other posets, including $V$-shaped posets, remains an open question. This study extends previous work by determining the minimum size $s(P)$ needed for an antichain star-like poset $P$ to have a sufficiently large subset $ \mathcal{Q}_{s(P)}  $ such that $ \mathcal{Q}_{s(P)}  $ contains a ramified copy of $P$. Additionally, it investigates the embeddability of $V$-shaped posets within two-colored subgraphs.

In the context of dynamic data streams, we investigate the $k$-center clustering problem and address the challenge of maintaining an efficient solution as the number of data dimensions increases. We aim to balance memory usage with accuracy, specifically focusing on a scenario where updating a data point's position incurs a cost that can be varied. We develop an algorithm that, when there are $d$ dimensions and we pay a cost of $U$ per update, uses a memory of $O(\sqrt[4]{dU}k\log (k^2/\delta))$ to achieve a solution within a factor of $O(\sqrt{dU})$ of the optimal. Notably, this factor remains constant when $d$ and $U$ are small. We also present a more efficient $O(\sqrt{dU}k\log (k^2/\delta))$ memory version of the algorithm. We also establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{dU}k)$ for any randomized memory usage. We also present memory-efficient variants of the algorithm that achieve nearly optimal memory use while keeping the competitiveness within a factor of 4 of the optimal.

We've developed an innovative hierarchical approach to resolve certain open problems in the study of stochastic chase-and-evasion games in continuous space. These hasty-type games involve two players, 'Rogue' and 'Hawk,' who pursue each other at fixed speeds, maximizing their chances of capturing one another. Due to the infinite nature of the state and value functions, we apply a value-iteration procedure within a grid-based framework, where each level of the hierarchy refines the decomposition of the domain and function from the previous level. This method enables us to efficiently utilize Level N's computations for Level N+1, allowing for coarse levels to be computed on broader problem scales and finer levels to build upon them. We've demonstrated this approach's effectiveness through numerical results and a comparative analysis with existing methods, showcasing its versatility across various problem settings and starting points.

Probabilities arranged in a circle can sometimes create deceptive patterns, as certain configurations enable probabilities to cycle endlessly without a clear greater or lesser relationship when compared. However, there are also licit configurations that exhibit this cyclic behavior, but not with the usual fairness. Additionally, we found that there are settings where a clear greater or lesser relationship can be achieved, as some players can always expect a better outcome than others. These findings have a striking parallel to the psychological phenomenon of narcissism, where some individuals consistently expect a better outcome than others.

Recently, deep learning techniques have been widely used for low-dose CT image reconstruction due to reduced radiation exposure achieved through scan at low-dose settings. Most of these approaches are dependent on training data from CT scans taken at high-dose settings, which are typically used for diagnostic purposes. In this study, a novel AdaSwitch network was developed to enhance low-dose CT scans based on the CycleGAN framework, allowing the use of two sets of generators and discriminators to learn both forward and reverse mappings between two data distributions without requiring them to be identical. To address computational constraints, AdaSwitch network was created by selectively applying Adaaptive Instance Normalization layers in relevant domains during training. Experimental results on synthetic and real data demonstrate that AdaSwitch achieved high-quality reconstruction results comparable to other advanced methods, while being relatively computationally efficient.

Recently, pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success in various NLP tasks through task-specific fine-tuning. However, these approaches fall short when dealing with large numbers of under-represented labels. We introduce a novel training framework, SPACE-2, that combines tree-structured contrastive pre-training with semi-supervised learning. This allows for the efficient use of vast amounts of unlabeled data. We harnessed the benefits of the HuggingFace Datasets and pre-trained models to fine-tune the HPB dialog understanding task with a high degree of label sparsity. Our experiment showed that even with a 99% unlabeled data ratio, the model reached state-of-the-art performance with only 1% of the labels.

This research paper focuses on a specific type of manifold that represents a perfect fluid and is linked to a special soliton known as the conformal Ricci-Yamabe type. We demonstrate that the geometry of this manifold is indeed of the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton kind. Additionally, we establish that the geometry of this perfect fluid spacetime is not mutually exclusive to the formation of the described soliton.

To investigate the spin effects within rotating, distorted nuclei of a distorted halo type, we developed a Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory that accounts for rotation in the cranking framework. This theoretical model features a decoupling term that captures the spin decoupling. In the absence of the decoupling term, the model transforms into a standard time-dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov model. We incorporated a Gaussian decoupling term to analyze spin effects in rotating $^{11}$Be nuclei with different shapes. The rotating $^{11}$Be nucleus exhibits a shape decoupling term that varies with rotation speed, exhibiting both positive and negative values. The model reveals that the decoupling strength has significant impacts on the nuclei's deformation and intrinsic properties, particularly on the angular momentum and aligned spin. Notably, the effects of the spin decoupling term are amplified by approximately a factor of 30 in rotating nuclei compared to non-rotating nuclei.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the bidirectional propagation method, which can be improved by incorporating external information from neighboring frames to align and propagate data more effectively. In video super-resolution, the BVSR model utilizes this method, but it suffers from imperfect alignment due to motion estimation inaccuracies and propagates high-frequency noise from low-resolution frame inputs, limiting performance gains.
